The official Telegram page for Mojtaba Khamenei has released details of two meetings Iran's supreme leader has reportedly held in recent days.
According to the readout, he met with the head of Iran's judiciary, Gholamhossein Mohseni-Ejei, on Saturday, during which the two reportedly discussed pursuing compensation from the U.S. and Israel over damages from the war in Iran. articles.title: Saudi-led coalition thwarts wave of Houthi attacks on kingdom
articles.summary: The Saudi-led coalition against Houthis said Tuesday it intercepted wave of ballistic missiles and drones targeting two regions in Saudi Arabia, as the conflict with the Iran-align...
articles.full_text:
The Saudi-led coalition against Houthis said Tuesday it intercepted wave of ballistic missiles and drones targeting two regions in Saudi Arabia, as the conflict with the Iran-aligned group intensifies.
The Houthis launched three ballistic missiles toward Saudi Arabia's Eastern Region and four drones toward the country's Southern Region, the coalition said.
Saudi Civil Defense issued early warnings for a potential threat in the Eastern Region and in Kharj governorate, later saying the danger had passed in both areas.
Saudi Arabia has intensified its strikes on the Houthis since the group captured strategic areas along Yemen's Red Sea coast last month, advancing toward the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a key global shipping route for Gulf oil producers opposite the Strait of Hormuz on the Arabian Peninsula.
Earlier Monday, the coalition said it intercepted and destroyed three drones over the Riyadh region and southern Saudi Arabia, without identifying their origin or intended targets.
The coalition also announced strikes on Houthi positions in Yemen, saying it destroyed ballistic missile launchers, storage tunnels and a missile depot.
Coalition spokesperson Turki al-Maliki said the operations aimed to dismantle the group's ballistic missile network and disrupt its supply routes.
The renewed fighting between the two sides has shattered a 2022 U.N.-brokered truce that largely halted attacks between the Saudi-led coalition, which backs Yemen's internationally recognized government, and the Houthis, who control the capital Sanaa.
The escalation has also opened another front in regional conflicts involving the U.S., Israel and Iran.

articles.title: The Houthis Continue to Threaten with Missiles—Has Saudi Arabia “Surrendered” to Iran? - Atalayar
articles.summary: The Houthis Continue to Threaten with Missiles—Has Saudi Arabia “Surrendered” to Iran?  Atalayar
articles.full_text:
A statement issued by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and reported by the Saudi Press Agency (WAAS) noted that: “As an extension of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia’s role in fostering dialogue and regional and international peace, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs confirms that the visit by Prince Khalid bin Salman bin Abdulaziz, Minister of Defense, and representatives of the countries of the Mecca Mutual Defense Agreement to the Iranian capital, Tehran, to meet with senior Iranian officials, falls within the framework of the ongoing efforts by the countries of the Mecca Agreement, the Joint Defense Agreement, to de-escalate tensions between the parties to the current crisis, promote dialogue and diplomatic solutions, and support the mediation efforts undertaken by the State of Qatar and the Islamic Republic of Pakistan.”
However, on-the-ground reports and independent sources reveal that the visit comes after Riyadh realized the impossibility of militarily defeating the Yemeni Houthis, following unprecedented attacks by the Iran-backed group against the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia.
Saudi Arabia tops the list of countries with the highest military spending in the Middle East and among Arab nations, at approximately $83.2 billion in 2025, while the 2026 state budget allocated approximately 240 billion riyals ($64 billion) to the military sector, according to defense budget estimates.
Despite this, Saudi Arabia failed to counter the threat from the Houthis, who announced that they were targeting an air base and a naval base in southern Saudi Arabia with “dozens of ballistic missiles,” in addition to Riyadh Airport, where aircraft were taking off and landing, according to their website.
Disruption in Saudi Arabia
Houthi spokesperson Yahya Saif stated that the group carried out “three significant operations involving dozens of ballistic missiles” at Riyadh Airport, Khalid Air Base in Khamis Mushait (south), and the Southern Naval Base of the Border Guard Forces in Jizan, where “the strike was precise, causing several deaths and injuries among Saudi enemy officers and soldiers.”
The closure of Riyadh Airport following the Houthi attacks dealt a major blow to the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, as a major investment conference and other events were canceled. Residents were forced to find alternative ways to travel.
Saudi officials did not provide additional information when the AFP news agency inquired about the resumption of flights at the airport. However, the flight-tracking website “Flight Radar” showed a small number of departures and the cancellation of a large number of flights, while the International Automobile Federation (FIA) announced on Saturday that the 2027 Saudi Dakar Rally, scheduled to take place from January 1 to 15, will not be held in Saudi Arabia due to events in the region.
The Asian Football Confederation also announced on Sunday the postponement of the match between the Saudi Arabia and United Arab Emirates national teams, scheduled for Monday in Riyadh, as part of the third round of the Asian Champions League.
The Stage Leading Up to the Collapse
Political analyst Abdul Qader Abu Lim asserts that “thanks to the betrayals of the Yemeni Reformist Brotherhood Party—which has been co-opted into the current Saudi system—Riyadh’s decisions are being condoned, even as it suffers the loss of powerful allies.”
He noted in a post that: “The Houthis managed to shift the battle from the stage of ‘breaking bones’ to the stage of pushing the Saudi regime toward war on the brink of the abyss—which is the final stage of the war before collapse—and this is what prompted the Saudi regime to visit Tehran, perhaps in hopes of finding a solution there.”
For his part, Yemeni journalist Fikri Saleh Hamlan asked: “How can Saudi Arabia sideline its sincere allies in Yemen, the South, and the United Arab Emirates, and meet with those who launched their planes and drones against them?”
He asserted in a post that “what is happening is not political maneuvering, but rather total submission to the conditions dictated by opponents following defeat on the ground and the loss of a reliable ally.”
Pakistan played a dual role, serving as both a staunch partner of Riyadh and an indirect channel of communication between Washington and Tehran, but the fighting that has erupted between the Iran-aligned Houthi group in Yemen and Saudi forces is increasingly testing the extent to which Islamabad can continue to play both roles simultaneously.
According to Reuters, this conflict marks the first major test of the joint defense alliance signed by Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Turkey in August, as well as an existing defense agreement between Islamabad and Riyadh. Under this agreement, any armed attack against any of the three countries is considered an attack on all of them, but so far, the alliance has not been visible on the ground, while Saudi Arabia remains under fire from Houthi missiles.
Pakistani officials fear that Houthi threats could put Islamabad at greater risk of being dragged into the war following Iranian missile strikes against Saudi energy facilities earlier this year, according to Reuters.
The Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia put this agreement to its first serious test, at a time when Riyadh is trying to prevent the clashes from spreading to its vital infrastructure.
Sources reveal that the visit by the parties to the Mecca Agreement is not for diplomatic purposes, as the Houthi attacks forced Riyadh to seek mediation after it failed to deter the group controlling Sana’a.
A Blow to the Allies
Meanwhile, these developments come after the Saudi kingdom turned against its allies in Yemen. This affects the United Arab Emirates and local powers, following the sacrifices they made to secure the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia.
The United Arab Emirates and the southern powers—led by the Southern Transitional Council and its affiliated forces, such as the Security Belt, the Giants Brigades, and elite forces—played a pivotal role in the military and security landscape of southern Yemen.
Securing the southern governorates after their liberation was a major priority for the United Arab Emirates, especially since the temporary capital, Aden, and its surrounding areas experienced a significant security vacuum due to the war launched by the Houthi militia.
In 2016, the United Arab Emirates and local forces expelled al-Qaeda from Mukalla, the capital of Hadhramaut, after a year of control. The oil-rich province shares a direct border with Saudi Arabia to the north.
Following Saudi Arabia’s strike against its allies in late 2025, when southern forces were bombed, Erik Kalinak, Slovakia’s representative to the European Parliament warned that the withdrawal of Emirati forces from southern Yemen had created a dangerous security vacuum, threatening the world’s most vital shipping route—the Red Sea.
Speaking in the European Parliament, Kalinak noted that “when we talk about security, we simply cannot ignore the situation in Yemen. Emirati forces have withdrawn from the south and have just pulled out their last counterterrorism units, and this has created a dangerous vacuum in the world’s most important vital shipping route.”
In Saudi Arabia’s first test following the United Arab Emirates’ withdrawal, its forces retreated in the face of the Houthi group, which controlled only the western coast in the Bab al-Mandab area. Aden became a temporary capital with the landing of United Arab Emirates soldiers, who spearheaded the city’s liberation. The vanguard of the Emirati special forces participated in the liberation of Aden International Airport and in organizing the southern resistance forces against the Houthi militias and the Muslim Brotherhood’s infiltration, which enabled them to extend their control over the southern regions.

articles.title: Houthis hit Saudi refinery as Iran warns of ‘devastating’ response to further US-Israeli attacks - Middle East Eye
articles.summary: Houthis hit Saudi refinery as Iran warns of ‘devastating’ response to further US-Israeli attacks  Middle East Eye
articles.full_text:
Yemen’s Ansar Allah group, known as the Houthis, said on Tuesday that it had struck Saudi Arabia’s Ras Tanura oil refinery, the kingdom’s largest.
The group’s military spokesperson, Yahya Saree, said a ballistic missile ignited a fire at the Gulf‑side facility, west of the Strait of Hormuz, though Saudi authorities have not confirmed the attack.
The Houthis have intensified strikes on Saudi territory since Riyadh hit Sanaa’s international airport in July, breaking a ceasefire and opening another front in the wider US-Israeli war on Iran.
Saudi Arabia sends almost all its oil exports through two main ports: Ras Tanura on the Gulf and Yanbu on the Red Sea. The Houthis have previously attacked Yanbu.
Bloomberg News reported on Tuesday, citing a source familiar with the matter, that Saudi Arabia had contained a fire near the Ras Tanura oil terminal earlier that day.
Separately, Saudi‑backed Yemeni forces said they had carried out 1,276 operations against Houthi positions in the past 24 hours as part of their “Dawn of Yemen” offensive.
Military spokesperson Colonel Majed al‑Nuzaili said the operations had “neutralised” about 382 Houthi commanders and fighters, without specifying how many were killed or wounded.
He added that the forces had destroyed or damaged 140 military vehicles and heavy weapons, as well as several arms and ammunition depots, and had struck Houthi command centres, defensive positions, reinforcements and supply routes across several fronts.
The US Embassy in Riyadh has told non-emergency government employees and their families to leave Saudi Arabia due to safety risks, an order first issued on 23 October.
In a statement on X, the embassy warned of possible further attacks on airports, airspace closures, flight cancellations and travel disruption.
'US inability to provide security'
In Iran, Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council Mohsen Rezaei met Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei on Tuesday, state media reported. Khamenei has not appeared in public since succeeding his father, Ali Khamenei, who Israeli-US forces assassinated on 28 February.
Rezaei’s meeting followed talks on Monday with members of the Mecca Alliance - Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, Pakistan’s army chief Asim Munir and Turkey’s intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin - as regional states are seeking to end the war.
“Washington’s inability to provide security guarantees has become evident,” Rezaei wrote on X on Tuesday.
“Security in West Asia must originate from within the region itself, and any foreign intervention must be prevented.”
On Monday, at a campaign rally in Corinth, Mississippi, US President Donald Trump defended the war as he faced poor opinion polls ahead of elections that could cost Republicans control of both houses of Congress. He repeated a Republican lawmaker’s false claim that “we didn’t start the war with Iran. Iran started the war with us”.
Trump also defended the war’s economic effects, saying he had expected oil prices to rise much higher.
“I was fully prepared to do it because we really had no choice. Should’ve been done a long time ago,” he said.
Trump said he had never supported ceasefire earlier in the year.
“We did a little ceasefire, which I never liked very much,” he said. “We wanna be nice, but it was just a waste of time as far as I’m concerned.”
He added that Iran had developed missiles capable of reaching Europe and potentially targeting US cities.
'An unstable regional system has been constructed on the entirely false perception that there is a fundamental regional antagonism between Iran and the Arab states of the Gulf'
- Badr al-Busaidi, Omani foreign minister
On Tuesday, Abdollah Haji Sadeghi, Iran supreme leader’s representative to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, said Tehran knew “the enemy’s vulnerabilities”. He warned that further US attacks would draw a “harsher and more devastating” response, according to the semi-official Tasnim news agency.
Sadeghi said “the enemy” had wrongly assumed that assassinating Iranian leaders and military commanders would turn public opinion against the government.
After failing militarily, he said, “the enemy” was now using psychological warfare to create “despair, stoking divisions, and casting doubt on resistance”.
Speaking in Cambridge during a diplomatic visit to the UK, Oman's Foreign Minister Badr al-Busaidi called on Gulf states to form a non-aggression pact with Iran, and end the region's reliance on a failed US security umbrella.
"Instead of a genuine security structure designed to maintain stable relations between the eight states of the Gulf, an unstable regional system has been constructed on the entirely false perception that there is a fundamental regional antagonism between Iran and the Arab states of the Gulf," al-Busaidi said.
"There is no such fundamental antagonism. There are problems, yes, of course. But the plain fact is that Arabs and Persians have lived in peace around the Gulf for centuries."

articles.title: Saudi Arabia offered Houthis $1 billion through Iran to stop attacks: Report - The Times of India
articles.summary: Saudi Arabia offered Houthis $1 billion through Iran to stop attacks: Report  The Times of India
articles.full_text:
Saudi Arabia has reportedly offered $1 billion to Yemen's Houthi group under an Iran-brokered arrangement aimed at securing a ceasefire and stopping attacks on the kingdom, Israeli media reported, citing diplomatic sources in the Gulf.
According to the reports, Saudi defence minister Prince Khalid bin Salman travelled to Tehran for talks on a possible ceasefire with the Houthis. The proposed arrangement reportedly involved transferring $1 billion to the group through Iran.
One diplomatic source claimed that the Saudi minister had even brought the money to Tehran aboard the Hercules military transport aircraft he arrived in. However, a Saudi official did not confirm that any money had been transferred, the reports said.
The talks reportedly brought together Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin and Pakistan's army chief 
Asim Munir
, alongside Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, Supreme National Security Council Secretary General Mohsen Rezaei and senior officials from the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).
According to the reports, Iran offered to mediate between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis amid escalating attacks on Saudi airports and oil facilities, which have caused economic damage to the kingdom. 
Iranian attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz have also disrupted oil exports from the Gulf, adding to regional instability.
The Saudi foreign ministry addressed the visit in an official statement, saying, "The visit to Tehran by Prince Khalid bin Salman, the defence minister, and representatives of the member states of the Mecca Joint Defence Alliance comes as part of the 'Nato-style' alliance's ongoing efforts to de-escalate tensions between the parties to the current crisis, encourage dialogue and diplomatic solutions, and support the mediation efforts undertaken by the State of Qatar and the Islamic Republic of Pakistan."
A Saudi official, speaking to Israeli media, did not confirm the reported financial transfer but said that part of the dispute with the Houthis centred on the implementation of understandings reached three years ago.
Under those understandings, Saudi Arabia was to provide direct financial assistance to the Houthis as part of efforts to reach a settlement. The funding was intended, among other purposes, to pay public-sector salaries in areas under Houthi control and rebuild civilian infrastructure. In return, the group was expected to maintain the ceasefire and stop attacks on Saudi Arabia, the reports said.
In recent months, the Houthis have sought to justify their "attacks" by alleging that Saudi Arabia reneged on the earlier understandings.
However, the Saudi position reportedly remains that the kingdom will not agree to a new ceasefire under "military blackmail". Israeli media reported that Riyadh also opposed transferring funds to the Houthis before they returned territory seized from Yemen's internationally recognised government, which Saudi Arabia backs.
The reported negotiations come amid wider regional tensions involving Iran, the United States and Israel. Tehran has sought to strengthen its regional influence while promoting a security framework led by regional powers.
According to Israeli media, the Tehran meeting also marked the first official meeting between representatives of the Mecca Joint Defence Alliance and the Iranian leadership. The initiative reportedly took shape during the Pakistani army chief's visit to Tehran the previous week.
The reports said Iran was seeking to position itself as a regional diplomatic mediator while opposing US or Israeli military intervention in the region.
The reported $1 billion proposal, including the claim that the money was brought to Tehran aboard the Saudi minister's aircraft, has not been independently confirmed.

articles.title: Why Saudi Arabia helped create its worst Houthi nightmare – opinion - World Israel News
articles.summary: Why Saudi Arabia helped create its worst Houthi nightmare – opinion  World Israel News
articles.full_text:
For other Middle Eastern governments, the lesson is not that military strength is irrelevant, but that it cannot substitute for political strategy.
By Amine Ayoub, Middle East Forum
Saudi Arabia’s wealth and advanced military arsenal were supposed to shield the kingdom from threats across its southern border.
Yet renewed Houthi attacks have exposed the limits of that confidence.
In October 2026, an attack on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport reportedly killed at least 13 people and wounded more than 300, while a strike on an Aramco administrative building in Dhahran caused a limited fire.
Houthi claims about other Saudi targets have not all been independently verified.
Even so, the combination of infrastructure risks and threats to Red Sea shipping shows how an adversary with fewer resources can impose heavy costs on a much wealthier state.
The Houthi movement, officially known as Ansar Allah, did not emerge overnight, and its rise cannot be explained entirely by Iran.
Its roots lie in Yemen’s domestic politics, religious competition, and regional rivalries. Saudi Arabia did not start the movement, but its policies helped shape the environment in which it grew.
The 2015 intervention gave the movement fresh grievances to exploit without eliminating its ability to fight.
For decades, Riyadh treated Yemen as a strategic buffer. Religious outreach became one instrument of its policy.
Saudi-backed Salafi institutions expanded into areas where Zaydism, a distinct branch of Shia Islam, had deep roots.
This competition did not make armed conflict inevitable, but it sharpened anxieties over identity and political authority.
The establishment of Dar al-Hadith in Dammaj around 1980 marked an important stage in Salafism’s spread in Saada.
Associated with Saudi-financed outreach, the center attracted students from Yemen and abroad.
To many Zaydi communities, institutions teaching a competing tradition threatened their established position.
Saudi policy was not the only driver, but it helped turn religious competition into a wider political issue.
The Believing Youth movement emerged in this environment. Founded in 1992 by Zaydi religious figures, it initially promoted religious education and cultural revival.
Hussein Badreddin al-Houthi joined in 1999 and helped shift it toward politics.
Its appeal reflected not only opposition to Saudi influence but also local grievances, underdevelopment, disputes over state authority, and dissatisfaction with President Ali Abdullah Saleh.
Many Zaydis did not initially support the Houthis; their expansion depended on political choices and alliances, not religious identity alone.
The conflict became militarized in 2004, when the Yemeni government moved against Hussein al-Houthi and his followers.
Six rounds of fighting followed in Saada through 2010. The campaigns failed to eradicate the insurgency and deepened hostility.
Hussein’s death did not end the rebellion; his brother Abdul-Malik eventually became its leader. The movement survived and portrayed itself as defender of communities neglected by the central government.
Saudi policy did not create the Houthi movement, but it helped intensify the conditions in which it grew.
Religious competition reinforced sectarian anxieties and weakened confidence in the state’s neutrality.
Riyadh was not responsible for every Houthi decision, yet it bears responsibility for the strategic consequences of its long approach to Yemen.
The decisive regional turning point came in March 2015. After the Houthis seized Sanaa in September 2014 and President Abdrabbuh Mansur Hadi’s government lost control of the capital, Saudi Arabia launched Operation Decisive Storm under Defense Minister Mohammed bin Salman.
Riyadh said it would restore the internationally recognized government. The campaign relied heavily on airpower and Western-supplied equipment, but tactical superiority did not translate into political success.
The intervention treated a complex local insurgency as a conventional military target that airpower could degrade into submission. Instead, it became a prolonged war.
The Saudi-led coalition’s air campaign damaged civilian infrastructure, while import restrictions, economic collapse, and fighting worsened Yemen’s humanitarian crisis.
The Houthis also committed abuses and repressed people under their control. Responsibility for Yemen’s suffering extends across the conflict’s participants.
Still, international criticism of the coalition’s conduct undermined the claim that military pressure would quickly restore stability.
The intervention furnished the Houthis with a powerful narrative of resistance to foreign aggression.
This framing did not excuse their authoritarian rule or domestic abuses, but helped them present the war as a defense of national sovereignty.
State collapse and captured government weapons gave them resources beyond those of a local insurgency. Fighting provided experience, and the prolonged conflict accelerated their adaptation.
Iran’s role grew increasingly important. Tehran gained a partner able to threaten Saudi interests at relatively low cost.
United Nations investigators have documented Iranian-linked technical assistance, training, weapons, and financial support for systems the Houthis could not produce independently at scale.
Yet the movement was not manufactured in Tehran. Its local roots, captured stocks, battlefield learning, and exploitation of fractured institutions expanded its reach.
Iranian support amplified an existing actor rather than creating one.
The imbalance is increasingly economic as well as military. Saudi Arabia has invested in aircraft and air defenses, while the Houthis have relied on dispersed sites, drones, missiles, and tactics designed to complicate detection and interception.
The attacker does not need to destroy every target to impose costs: uncertainty can disrupt flights, raise insurance premiums, unsettle investors, and force authorities to devote resources to protecting infrastructure.
Such effects do not mean Saudi defenses are useless or that every attack succeeds.
They show instead that defending a large, open economy against repeated low-cost threats is a different task from winning a conventional campaign, and one that demands political as well as military tools.
By the early 2020s, war’s costs pushed Riyadh toward de-escalation. Oman helped facilitate contacts, and the 2022 United Nations-brokered truce reduced fighting without settling Yemen’s political future.
Saudi-Houthi talks in 2023 raised hopes of a wider agreement, but bilateral understandings could not reconcile Yemen’s competing authorities or guarantee that the Houthis would relinquish regional capabilities. A pause was not a durable peace.
The renewed confrontation also exposes how fragile the diplomatic track remains. In July 2026, the United Nations envoy held meetings in Riyadh and Muscat urging de-escalation and preservation of the truce’s gains.
The new fighting shows that contacts have not produced a durable framework.
Without a broader Yemeni-led settlement covering security, governance, and economic priorities, ongoing local battles can again trigger regional consequences.
The dilemma is that neither pressure nor accommodation has yet produced a durable outcome.
Airstrikes can damage Houthi infrastructure but cannot settle who governs Yemen; a bilateral truce can reduce danger but leave rivals vulnerable and the movement armed.
Without monitoring, security guarantees and a political process that includes Yemen’s own factions, each side has reason to rebuild its position and prepare to fight again.
The consequences extend beyond Yemen. Threats to Red Sea shipping raise costs for commercial operators and draw outside powers into a locally rooted conflict.
Attacks on Saudi facilities challenge the assumption that expensive defense systems can protect every site across a vast territory.
Interception matters, but so do intelligence, resilient infrastructure, diplomacy, and a settlement that reduces incentives for renewed attacks.
Alignments are rarely permanent, and local partners may pursue goals that diverge from those of their patrons.
A policy designed to preserve influence can intensify rivalries, while war can give an adversary credibility, experience, and new means of retaliation.
The House of Saud did not manufacture the Houthis. But Saudi-backed religious competition aggravated tensions in northern Yemen, and the 2015 intervention gave an established movement further opportunities to mobilize and expand its reach.
Decisions intended to preserve regional influence helped strengthen a threat that proved difficult to contain.
Saudi Arabia can reduce its exposure through diplomacy and a serious Yemeni political process, but a ceasefire cannot endure if it leaves the country’s power struggle unresolved.
Wealth can buy aircraft and diplomatic influence; it cannot purchase consent or guarantee political success through force. Riyadh’s nightmare is not merely the Houthi arsenal.
It is that strategic choices helped strengthen an adversary whose consequences continue to outlast the policies that produced them.

articles.title: Egypt authorises military support for Saudi Arabia as Houthi militia attacks escalate - TRT World
articles.summary: Egypt authorises military support for Saudi Arabia as Houthi militia attacks escalate  TRT World
articles.full_text:
Egypt’s parliament has authorised the country’s military to provide support for Saudi Arabia’s defence, lawmakers and local media reported, potentially bringing Cairo closer to a regional conflict intensified by attacks from Yemen’s Houthi militia.
President Abdel Fattah el Sisi asked parliament last week to approve military assistance if Riyadh requests help defending itself against the Houthis, whose operations threaten Saudi territory and the strategic Bab al Mandab Strait, a vital shipping passage linking the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and access to Egypt’s Suez Canal.
The parliamentary authorisation comes as attacks on Saudi Arabia have disrupted aviation and oil exports, raising concerns over regional security and international trade routes.
Cairo draws a line around its military role
Egypt has repeatedly condemned Iranian and Iran-backed attacks on Gulf countries but has not publicly joined direct combat in the current conflict.
Sisi has indicated that any Egyptian support would be limited to defending Saudi territory and borders, rather than launching attacks inside Yemen.
Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty and intelligence chief Hassan Rashad travelled to Riyadh last Wednesday to deliver a letter from Sisi to Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman.
Following the visit, Abdelatty said Cairo supported exploring “every opportunity” to resolve the Yemen conflict through diplomacy.
Egypt’s potential involvement would mark a significant development given its military capabilities and strategic position along the Red Sea.
The country has also been considering joining a mutual defence pact involving Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Türkiye, signed in August.
Abdelatty said earlier this month that Egyptian membership remained “under serious consideration.”
A history of involvement in Yemen
Egypt joined the Saudi-led coalition supporting Yemen’s internationally recognised government in March 2015, primarily as a naval partner tasked with protecting Red Sea shipping lanes.
Cairo sent warships, pledged air support and deployed around 800 ground troops, although its direct combat role remained limited.
The country has a difficult history of military intervention in Yemen, having suffered heavy costs during its involvement in the 1960s. It has not undertaken a large-scale foreign ground deployment since the 1991 Gulf War.
Saudi Arabia remains a key political and financial partner for Cairo, providing billions of dollars in assistance, central bank deposits and energy supplies during Sisi’s presidency.
Red Sea security raises regional stakes
The latest escalation has added another volatile front to the wider US-Israeli war on Iran. The Houthis, who control Yemen’s capital, Sanaa, have attacked targets including Riyadh’s international airport and Saudi oil giant Aramco, disrupting flights and oil exports.
The conflict also threatens maritime traffic through the Bab al Mandab Strait, a strategic chokepoint for shipping travelling between the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden. Any sustained disruption could affect routes serving the Suez Canal, a major source of revenue for Egypt.
Saudi Arabia and Egypt have stepped up security discussions as the fighting intensifies. Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman visited Cairo on September 15 to discuss security and navigation in the Red Sea.
The extent of any Egyptian military support will depend on Saudi Arabia’s requests and how Cairo balances its security commitments with efforts to prevent further regional escalation.

articles.title: Houthis claim fresh attacks on Saudi Arabia, Aden - Aaj English TV
articles.summary: Houthis claim fresh attacks on Saudi Arabia, Aden  Aaj English TV
articles.full_text:
4 min read
Yemen’s Houthis launched fresh attacks on Saudi Arabia and the seat of Yemen’s internationally recognised government on Saturday after blaming the kingdom for strikes that the Iran-backed group said killed 17 people.
Saudi Arabia and the government it backs in Yemen have come under sustained attack in recent weeks from the Houthis as a years-long truce broke down in the summer, shifting the focus of the wider US-Iran war that erupted in February.
Over the past 24 hours, the Yemeni fighters said they targeted three Saudi airports, including the international airport in the capital Riyadh, energy installations, a pipeline and an air base.
Military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group launched missiles at “King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, the capital of the Saudi enemy, in two phases”, the airports in Dammam in the east and Najran in the south.
The group also launched attacks on the southern Khamis Mushait air base as well as “crude oil pumping stations and the crude oil pipeline from east to west”.
The Saudi civil defence agency said it had also responded to falling debris in the holy cities of Makkah and Madinah regions on Saturday after intercepting two Houthi missiles. The Houthis denied targeting the cities, the two holiest in Islam, calling the Saudi claim a “huge lie”.
The Houthis also fired at the southern Yemeni city of Aden, the interim seat of the Saudi-backed government, saying they targeted a naval base and military camp overseen by Saudi forces.
Authorities said the coast guard headquarters and a second building of theirs, as well as Aden airport, had been targeted.
The fresh attack claims came after the Houthis’ Al-Masirah TV channel accused the kingdom of separate strikes in Yemen that killed more than a dozen people. Riyadh has not claimed the alleged strikes.
The Houthi broadcaster said a strike on a house in Sanaa killed at least four people, another at a residential building for cement factory workers killed eight and another outside the city of Hodeida killed five from the same family.
Yemen’s civil war, pitting the Iran-backed Houthis against the Saudi-supported and internationally recognised government, had been dormant since a ceasefire in 2022, but erupted again in July as the wider Middle East war roiled the region.
Diplomats evacuated
Earlier Saturday, the Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted two missiles targeting Saudi cities Taif and Yanbu in the kingdom’s west.
Saudi Arabia’s civil defence had broadcast warnings of “potential danger” for four western regions, including Taif and Yanbu as well as Makkah.
The warning was lifted minutes later.
The group has also targeted the kingdom’s oil infrastructure as well as its airports and tankers.
Yanbu is a major oil export hub on the Red Sea coast that has allowed Riyadh to bypass Iran’s blockade of the Strait of Hormuz for much of its crude exports via the east-west pipeline.
An attack on Riyadh airport earlier this month killed 13 people and forced it to shut, while this week the US ordered non-essential embassy staff and their families to leave Saudi Arabia, citing the Houthi threat.
Riyadh leads a military coalition that first intervened in 2015 in the conflict, which has devastated Yemen and created one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises.
The dramatic escalation in Yemen, with the Houthis taking control of the entire Red Sea coast in a lightning offensive last month, has further destabilised the region and disrupted oil markets.
In July, a fragile 2022 truce fell apart after the Houthis allowed an Iranian plane to land in Yemen’s capital Sanaa in defiance of Saudi control over Yemeni airspace, setting off a spate of attacks.
The Houthis then declared a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia and began hitting its ships, territory and oil facilities, before launching a major offensive in September in which they seized Yemeni government-held territory along the Red Sea coast.
In response, the Houthis have also reported frequent Saudi strikes targeting areas under their control.
Egypt has suggested sending troops to help defend Saudi Arabia, while Britain and France have offered their forces to protect the Gulf kingdom.
On Saturday the US Mission to the United Arab Emirates and US embassy in Riyadh said Washington’s travel advisories for both Gulf countries were “updated to reflect an increase in potential armed attacks by the Iranian-supported Houthis”.

articles.title: Houthis Claim Attacks on Saudi Oil Pumps and Riyadh Airport - Breitbart News
articles.summary: Houthis Claim Attacks on Saudi Oil Pumps and Riyadh Airport  Breitbart News
articles.full_text:
The Iran-backed Houthi insurgents of Yemen on Monday claimed drone attacks on the oil pumping stations along Saudi Arabia’s vital East-West Pipeline, plus a new missile attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, just hours after it resumed limited operations following a previous Houthi missile attack.
The East-West Pipeline runs about 750 miles from the refineries of Abqaiq to the Red Sea port of Yanbu. It has become a vital part of Saudi Arabia’s effort to bypass the menace of Iranian terrorism in the Strait of Hormuz by shipping oil through the Red Sea.
The pipeline was attacked by the Houthis in mid-September, prompting a safety shutdown for about two weeks. It has since returned to pumping oil at nearly its optimum capacity. There was no immediate confirmation of damage to the pumping system from Saudi Arabia’s national oil company, Aramco.
The Houthis also took responsibility for launching a ballistic missile at King Khalid International Airport in the Saudi capital city of Riyadh. The Saudi military coalition said it intercepted the missile and destroyed two ballistic missile launchers near Yemen’s capital of Sanaa, which the Houthis occupied in 2014.
The coalition claimed it destroyed a total of four Houthi missile launchers on Monday, plus a missile storage facility and underground tunnels where missiles were stored.
The Houthis claimed they launched “dozens of ballistic missiles” at Riyadh, and the strike on the airport “achieved its target.”
“The Yemeni Armed Forces warn all international, regional and local airlines – as well as staff and travellers – against using King Khalid Airport in Riyadh, as it is unsafe and serves as a military target for our forces,” said Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree.
“The Saudi regime shall bear the consequences of any operations at the airport,” he added.
Saree claimed Saudi warplanes launched 56 strikes at targets in Yemen on Saturday and Sunday, all of them “targeting civilian objects.”
King Khalid International Airport had only just resumed limited flight operations following a Houthi attack on October 12 that killed 13 people and wounded over 300. Although eyewitnesses in Riyadh reported hearing explosions, Saudi officials refused to comment on whether the airport was damaged.
The Saudis have canceled several events and conferences due to Houthi attacks on their airports. On Sunday, the organizers of the Dakar Rally motor sports event announced they would move the race out of Saudi Arabia this year, to a venue in Africa.
The organizers, the Amaury Sport Organization (ASO), said the Dakar Rally would return to Saudi Arabia in 2027, just in time for its 50th anniversary event.

articles.title: Houthis test Trump by ramping up attacks on Saudi Arabia, developing ballistic missile tech - Just The News
articles.summary: Houthis test Trump by ramping up attacks on Saudi Arabia, developing ballistic missile tech  Just The News
articles.full_text:
Iran-backed group steps up attacks on Saudi Arabia and allegedly acquires Chinese parts to produce precision ballistic missiles.
The Iran-backed Houthis have exploited the regional chaos of the U.S.-Iran war and new technology to boost their power – and the threat they pose – to the United States and its partners in the Middle East.
President Trump has warned Yemen’s Houthis as the group steps up attacks on Saudi Arabia amid the Iran war, suggesting they could face dire consequences after the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
The attacks on Saudi oil and civilian infrastructure, including repeated strikes on commercial airports, have continued to roil global oil markets.
The attacks on Saudi Arabia even prompted the U.S. State Department to order on Wednesday all “non-emergency government employees and their family members” to leave the country.
Trump also thinks the Houthis have resumed their attacks at the request of Iran, a longtime backer of the group, to confound his efforts to bring the roughly eight-month-long Middle East war to a close.
“The Houthis are behaving very badly," Trump recently posted to Truth Social. "I thought they learned their lesson a year ago when we bombed the HELL out of them and, at their request, stopped. They’ve been silent for a long time, but now they’ve emerged again, probably at the behest of Iran … in a very nasty way, hitting Saudi Arabia, and purposefully trying to drive up Oil Prices, probably prior to the U.S. Elections – NOT NICE.
“Somebody should explain to them that I’m not running in the Elections, I’ve already won, IN A MASSIVE LANDSLIDE, but I’ll be there after the Elections, and I will never forget."
The Houthis, whose official name is Ansar Allah or Supporters of God, have controlled northwestern Yemen for years amid a civil war that has divided the Arabian country since 2014. The U.S.-designated terrorist group receives backing from Iran, including weapons and funding.
Early in Trump’s second term, the United States bombed the Houthis in retaliation for the group’s attacks on shipping in the Red Sea, which were launched in October 2023 in response to Israel’s war in Gaza.
The attacks first exposed the global markets, U.S. allies, and the United States to the threat the Houthis pose. Now, the group is using the war to boost its own capabilities and attack neighboring Saudi Arabia with devastating effect.
Since the Middle East was plunged into war, the Houthis have been quietly working to develop advanced ballistic missile capabilities that would allow the group to strike even deeper into Israel and Saudi Arabia – or at U.S. military bases in the Middle East. Such an advancement would be a major firepower upgrade for the Iran proxy, which at one time was more focused on Yemen’s internal affairs.
Conflict Armament Research, a group that studies and documents weapons in armed conflicts, recently released a report revealing the Houthis’ attempts to produce advanced medium-range ballistic missiles using Iranian designs and Chinese components.
The effort was discovered after authorities in the Saudi-backed Yemeni government intercepted two shipments last year coming from China. Those shipments contained components needed to construct a homegrown version of Iran’s Kheibar Shekan precision guided missile.
Iran has used the Kheibar Shekan to strike U.S. bases during the conflict, and was likely used in the July attack that killed three U.S. service members in Jordan.
According to the report, the seized cargo included custom-made metal components for the missile’s motor and airframe, along with stabilizing fins and solid-propellant rocket motor parts from the Kheibar Shekan series. Shipping documents traced the parts to an unnamed Chinese precision-metal manufacturer.
If the effort succeeds, the Houthi version would have a range of roughly 2,000 kilometers (about 1,200 miles), putting all of Saudi Arabia and Israel within striking distance.
“The local ambition of the Houthis for manufacturing is beyond what was previously assumed,” Fabian Hinz, senior analyst at Conflict Armament Research, told the Wall Street Journal. Hinz also told the outlet that the group conceals its weapons sites so well that it remains unclear how far production has advanced.
Further, there is evidence that the Houthis attempted to use advanced American Artificial Intelligence capabilities to test such missiles. In a threat report released last month, Anthropic identified “a cell of threat actors” using its signature Claude program to develop three new missiles with advanced capabilities in Yemen.
According to Anthropic, the “cell,” which the company does not explicitly identify with the Houthis, used the AI platform to develop a “guided rocket” with homing guidance capabilities, “a multi-stage ballistic missile” intended to achieve a range of 2,000 km, and “a multi-variant missile” that included a “hypersonic glide vehicle variant,” Just the News previously reported.
Meanwhile, the Houthis have made Saudi airports their primary target. Since early October, ballistic missile and drone strikes on airports in Riyadh, Abha, and Dammam have killed more than 20 people and injured hundreds. The deadliest strike came Oct. 10. At least 12 people were killed, including one American, and more than 300 were injured at Riyadh’s international airport.
On Wednesday, an attack on King Fahd International Airport in Dammam killed a Saudi national and an Indian resident. The Houthis claimed they also targeted Saudi Arabia’s defense ministry in Riyadh and Saudi Aramco facilities in Yanbu. Aramco reportedly ordered staff to evacuate its Dhahran headquarters, which was struck earlier this month.

articles.title: Iran president, Qatar emir meet on sidelines of Moscow summit

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Qatar’s Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani met Tuesday in Moscow to discuss expanding political, economic and energy ties, according to Iranian state media.
The talks took place on the sidelines of the eighth Gas Exporting Countries Forum summit. The intergovernmental organization brings together major natural gas-producing nations, including Iran, Russia, Qatar and Algeria.
Iranian state television reported that the leaders "reviewed the current state of relations between Tehran and Doha and emphasized the importance of deepening political and economic ties and making use of existing potential to strengthen bilateral cooperation."
The official IRNA news agency added that discussions included strengthening coordination among gas-exporting countries.
State media reports, however, made no mention of the ongoing Middle East war, which began with Feb. 28 U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran. Tehran responded to those attacks with missile and drone strikes across the region, including Qatar.
Qatar has played a central role in mediation efforts in recent months, working to end the regional conflict and facilitating ongoing negotiations between Iran and the U.S.
Pezeshkian is scheduled to meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin later Tuesday. In an Instagram post, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said the talks will follow up on discussions held during Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov's Oct. 19 visit to Tehran.
In early October, Putin stated that Russia is also prepared to help mediate an end to the war in the Middle East.

articles.title: Egypt Weighs Diplomacy and Military Intervention in the Red Sea - Arab Center Washington DC

Egypt has several good reasons for wanting the conflict between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia to end. After losing billions of dollars in Suez Canal tolls during the 2023-2025 Israeli war on Gaza—when Yemen’s Iranian-backed Houthi rebels targeted ships in the Red Sea ostensibly heading to Israel—Egypt had hoped to recoup some of its lost revenue following the October 2025 ceasefire. Although tolls have slightly rebounded, ten months after the ceasefire, renewed fighting between the Houthis and Yemeni government forces, as well as Houthi attacks on Saudi oil infrastructure and shipping, have again adversely affected ship traffic in the Red Sea.
It might then come as little surprise that, on October 26, 2026, the Egyptian parliament approved Riyadh’s request for military help to quell further Houthi attacks. But military involvement in Yemen’s conflict carries huge risks for Cairo. Egyptians have bad memories of their military intervention in the Yemeni civil war in the 1960s and do not want to revisit that quagmire. The Houthis have demonstrated an ability to strike targets hundreds of miles away, and Egypt has no desire for its own infrastructure to be added to the target list. For these reasons, Egypt still prefers a diplomatic solution to the crisis and maintains contacts with Tehran and the various groups fighting in Yemen. Nevertheless, pressure from Saudi Arabia, one of Egypt’s main economic benefactors, seems to have been effective in Cairo’s decision to provide military assistance to the kingdom.
Deliberations Over the Saudi Request
On September 15, 2026, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman flew to Cairo to meet with Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi reportedly to find ways to strengthen relations between the two allies across areas of shared regional and international concern. There was some speculation that the Saudis were there to request Egyptian military support in response to the recent Houthi attacks on the kingdom. The absence of a public announcement after the talks suggested that military assistance from Cairo would not be forthcoming. However, the Houthi attacks on Riyadh airport on October 10, 2026, which killed at least 13 civilians, along with the group’s strikes on the state-run Aramco oil company, seem to have spurred the Saudis to request such assistance again.
The Houthi attacks on Riyadh airport seem to have spurred the Saudis to request such assistance again.
On October 13, Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty claimed that his country would respond positively to any Saudi request for help and might even join the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement signed by Turkey, Pakistan, and Saudi Arabia—though that move seems unlikely, as Egypt has been averse to forming formal alliances in the past. Nevertheless, on October 18, Sisi said he would request that parliament authorize the Egyptian military to come to the aid of Saudi Arabia. The same day, Abdelatty posted on X that he had discussed regional matters with Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan, emphasizing the importance of de-escalation, which appears to be Cairo’s preferred path.
Domestic Economic Concerns for Egypt
Economics have played a significant role in Cairo’s decision to provide military support to Saudi Arabia. Sisi earlier claimed that Egypt lost approximately $10 billion during Israel’s 2023-2025 war on Gaza. Because the Red Sea connects with the Suez Canal—an important shipping route for vessels transiting between Asia and the Mediterranean—Houthi strikes on ships in this waterway have directly affected the Egyptian economy. In the fiscal year ending in July 2023 (before the outbreak of the Israeli war on Gaza), Egypt earned $10.25 billion in revenue from canal tolls. This figure dropped dramatically over the next two years, reaching around $4 billion in fiscal year (FY) 2024/2025 and $4.67 billion in FY2025/2026.
To be sure, Egypt receives foreign exchange from other sources, namely tourism and worker remittances, which have shown steady growth. The former brought in $15.3 billion in 2024, and the latter shows impressive growth. Remittances from Egyptians working abroad reached a record high of $33.9 billion in the first eight months of 2026. Although these sources of foreign exchange earnings exceed toll revenues from the Suez Canal, remittances generally accrue to households rather than to the state.
Nevertheless, Egypt’s financial needs are enormous. In FY2025/2026, the country’s total external debt reached $164.8 billion, up 5.2 percent from a year earlier, while the Central Bank of Egypt projected that external debt-servicing obligations in 2026 would amount to $29.2 billion, including $23.8 billion in principal repayments and $5.4 billion in interest payments. These payments are a huge burden on the Egyptian economy. Interest payments alone were projected to consume half of all government expenditure in FY2025/2026. The country’s high debt burden has led to a sharp decrease in social spending in real terms. For example, healthcare and education spending has declined as a percentage of GDP for the past few years—all the more alarming in a country with an estimated population of 118 million people. Inflation has dropped from an average of 34 percent in 2023 to around 13.9 percent in 2026. However, stubbornly high prices for food and other commodities continue to put economic stress on the population. The current IMF loan program is expected to end in December 2026, and the government has stated that it has no plans to extend it. Any drop in foreign exchange earnings is therefore worrying.
Initial Hope for a Boost in Tolls but Worries Return
Following the October 2025 ceasefire in Gaza, Egypt was optimistic that it could recoup some of its revenue losses resulting from the conflict. In the last five months of 2025, tolls increased by 17.5 percent compared to the same period in 2024, and Osama Rabie, chairman of the Suez Canal Authority, predicted in December 2025 that revenues could increase to some $8 billion in FY2026/2027. On February 8, 2026, Rabie announced that revenues from the Suez Canal had reached $449 million since the beginning of the year, up from $368 million for the same period in 2025.
Cairo has reason to be worried about the Houthi attacks from northern Yemen
Initially, Egypt benefitted from the US-Israeli war on Iran, which began in late February 2026, as Iran began to strike oil facilities, tankers, and other vessels in the Gulf, effectively halting maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz. In response, Saudi Arabia began to export more oil via the East-West pipeline to its Red Sea port of Yanbu, with ships then transporting Saudi oil to Europe through the Suez Canal. In July 2026, Egypt earned $505 million in canal revenues—its highest monthly intake since December 2023. The same month, 526 oil tankers transited the canal—up from 485 in June. However, Egypt’s FY2025/2026 Suez Canal revenue is low compared with its $10.25 billion in canal revenues in FY2022/2023, before the Israeli war on Gaza. The Suez Canal Authority has since revised its predictions, now suggesting that the canal’s revenue intake for FY2026/2027 will be around $6 billion. Even that figure, however, is optimistic given the renewal of Houthi strikes in and around the Red Sea.
Cairo has reason to be worried about the Houthi attacks from northern Yemen, which began targeting Saudi ships and oil infrastructure on July 13, 2026, and escalated to the point that Riyadh suspended crude oil exports from Yanbu for more than two weeks in September. The Houthis claimed that they were responding to Saudi policies of restricting air and sea access to Houthi-controlled territory. However, they are probably also responsive to demands from Iran, which wants to maintain pressure on Saudi Arabia. In September 2026, Houthi forces moved south along the western coast of Yemen to take territory from the internationally recognized and Saudi-backed Yemeni government, threatening the Bab al-Mandab Strait—a vital choke point connecting the Arabian Sea to the Red Sea. Although the Houthis claimed that they were only targeting Saudi ships or ships transporting oil from Saudi ports, any violence in this region reduces vessel traffic generally and through Egypt’s Suez Canal.
No Good Options for Cairo
Egypt’s options to end this conflict are limited. For largely historical reasons, Egypt has been reluctant to send ground forces into Yemen and become bogged down in the country once again. Egyptians have lingering memories of their country’s military intervention in the Yemeni civil war from 1962 to 1967, during which it deployed between 55,000 and 70,000 Egyptian soldiers who found themselves trapped in a quagmire that some described as “Nasser’s Vietnam.” Tellingly, when Saudi Arabia assembled a large coalition of Sunni Muslim states in March 2015 to oppose the Houthis’ takeover of Sanaa and much of northern Yemen, Egypt participated only by sending limited air and naval assets off the Yemeni coast to shell Houthi-controlled territory. At the time, Egyptian officials denied press reports claiming that they had dispatched ground troops. Today, Egypt is still technically part of the anti-Houthi coalition, though after its brief participation in the 2015 campaign, it has avoided any further military involvement in Yemen.
If Egypt does decide to send a significant military force to Yemen, it may risk becoming the target of Houthi attacks. Given that the Houthis were able to strike Israel repeatedly from northern Yemen during the 2023-2025 war, they can feasibly do the same to Egypt. Given the fragile state of the Egyptian economy, the country cannot afford attacks on its lucrative tourism industry or other threats that might discourage foreign investors.

The Qatari delegation is attending the eighth GECF summit in Moscow on Tueaday, bringing together leaders of major gas-exporting countries to discuss global gas markets and energy cooperation.
Qatar’s Amir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani met Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian in Moscow on Tuesday on the sidelines of the eighth summit of the Gas Exporting Countries Forum (GECF).
The two leaders discussed expanding political and economic ties, including cooperation in energy and trade and coordination among gas-producing countries, Iranian media reported, citing Pezeshkian’s office.
Qatar’s Amir arrived in Moscow on Monday to attend the GECF summit, which brings together leaders of major gas-exporting countries to discuss energy cooperation and global gas markets.
Separately, Qatar’s Minister of State for Energy Affairs and QatarEnergy President and CEO Saad Sherida Al Kaabi met with Iran’s Acting Minister of Petroleum, Hamid Bovard, in Moscow on Tuesday, at the sidelines of the 28th Ministerial Meeting of the Gas Exporting Countries Forum (GECF).
“Discussions during the meeting focused on energy relations and cooperation between Qatar and Iran,” QatarEnergy said.
This marks the second round of energy talks between Qatar and Iran this month, following a meeting in Doha on 19 October during a visit by Iran’s acting Minister of Petroleum, Hamid Bovard, where the two officials discussed bilateral relations and cooperation in the energy sector.
Al Kaabi also held separate meetings with energy ministers from Algeria, Libya, Senegal and Venezuela, with discussions covering bilateral energy cooperation, the forum’s agenda and developments in global gas markets.
During Qatar’s participation at the 28th Ministerial Meeting of the Gas Exporting Countries Forum (GECF) in Moscow on Monday, ahead of Tuesday’s summit of GECF, Al Kaabi, called for the protection of energy infrastructure and shipping routes amid regional conflict.
Al Kaabi warned that disruptions in the Gulf could have far-reaching consequences for global trade and energy security, citing attacks on energy facilities and restrictions on shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.
Qatar’s own energy production facilities had been targeted in several attacks, Al Kaabi said, adding that production had been halted and Qatari liquefied natural gas (LNG) vessels faced severe restrictions on their movement through regional shipping routes.
“It is critical that we work together to protect energy infrastructure during times of conflict,” Al Kaabi said, calling for the protection of energy routes and maritime shipping lanes.
Qatar’s energy minister reaffirmed Qatar’s commitment to reliable energy supplies, particularly LNG, saying the country sought to “be a force for peace” while continuing to play an active role in global energy markets.

Natural gas remained a key part of a diversified global energy mix and a balanced energy transition, he said, adding: “Natural gas is here to stay.”

Canada and the United Arab Emirates signed a comprehensive trade agreement Tuesday aimed at reducing trade barriers and attracting investment, as Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney seeks to diversify economic partnerships amid strained relations with the United States.
Carney and Abu Dhabi Crown Prince Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan presided over the signing of the Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA), which aims to cut tariffs, reduce red tape and improve market access for businesses in both countries.
Carney has vowed to double Canada's non-U.S. trade over the next decade as President Donald Trump's tariffs have rippled through Canada's economy. Subsequent attempts for a deal with Washington have broken down, and that has pushed Carney to aggressively pursue trade pacts with countries from the Asia Pacific to Europe and the Middle East.
"Once fully implemented, the CEPA will reduce or eliminate tariffs on over 99% of current Canadian exports to the UAE. That means new markets for Canadian farmers growing pulses and canola, for manufacturers of industrial machinery and power generation equipment, for our world-class aerospace sector, and other Canadian innovators," The Prime Minister's Office said in a statement.
"The agreement will also address non-tariff barriers, create a more predictable environment for trade and investment, and expand market access for Canadian goods and services, including in the industrial, agricultural, forest, fish and seafood, environmental, and engineering sectors," it said, adding CEPA is expected to enter into force in 2027.
The two countries also signed preliminary agreements on energy, diplomatic and defence cooperation.
"We see considerable potential for our private sector, whether through improved market access for our exporters or access to investment opportunities in high-growth sectors such as logistics, communications, advanced technology and manufacturing - all of which will support our pursuit of a resilient, diversified and globally connected economy,” UAE's Foreign Trade Minister Thani Al Zeyoudi said in a statement.
He signed the CEPA deal with his Canadian counterpart Maninder Sidhu.
UAE is the largest Middle Eastern market for Canadian exports and is a big buyer of Canadian motor vehicles and parts, and machinery. Two-way trade between the countries was worth C$3.5 billion ($2.48 billion) last year. It has been growing at 10% annually for the last few years, according to government data.
The UAE last year also committed up to $50 billion in investment in Canada.
The signing is the last step before Canada’s Parliament can ratify the agreement, a Canadian government source said.

The Israeli army entered a fifth day of a large-scale offensive in Hebron Tuesday, displacing nearly 5,000 Palestinians from their homes.
The Hebron municipality said in a statement that 4,969 Palestinians from 780 families have been forcibly displaced from the Deir Bahha and al-Jilda areas since the Israeli military campaign began Friday.
Among those displaced are 336 infants, 441 elderly, 216 pregnant and nursing women, 44 people with disabilities and 312 people suffering from chronic illnesses, the statement said.
The municipality said the figures document families forced out from their homes since the start of the Israeli campaign amid growing humanitarian consequences, particularly for people requiring special care.
The army has shut all entrances to Hebron and surrounding villages since Friday following a shooting attack that killed two Israeli soldiers.
Türkiye's Anadolu Agency reported Palestinians being stopped, searched and mistreated by Israeli forces at military checkpoints near al-Jilda Roundabout.
Witnesses said new military reinforcements also arrived in Ein Deir Baha, where Israeli forces have taken over several Palestinian buildings and turned them into military posts.
According to the Palestinian Prisoner Society, the Israeli army has arrested 85 Palestinians across Hebron governorate since Friday.
Elsewhere in the occupied West Bank, Israeli forces arrested at least nine Palestinians in military raids and closed all main entrances to Ramallah.
In the northern West Bank, Israeli forces raided the eastern neighborhood of Jenin as well as the towns of Meithalun, Jaba and Qabatiya, arresting at least six Palestinians, according to local sources.
A Palestinian man was detained during a raid on Aqraba, southeast of Nablus, while Israeli forces stormed the southern al-Hawouz area of Qaffin in Tulkarm governorate and raided a home in the town’s western neighborhood.
In the central West Bank, Israeli forces closed all main entrances to Ramallah, including the Ein Sinya and Atara checkpoints, the Rawabi gate and the Nabi Saleh and Aboud gates, and set up additional checkpoints on alternative roads.
In Al-Bireh, the army turned a Palestinian home into a military post, held four residents inside and confiscated their phones, according to local sources.
Palestinian farmers were also expelled from their land in Turmus Ayya, north of Ramallah, while Israeli forces raided Tuqu southeast of Bethlehem with tracked military vehicles.
In Hebron governorate, Israeli forces also repeatedly raided the town of Taffuh and searched the homes of former prisoners.
Israeli troops assaulted a Palestinian man in the Hawara area south of Hebron before arresting him and his son, according to local sources.
Separately, Israeli occupiers set fire to three Palestinian vehicles early Tuesday in the village of Umm Safa, west of Ramallah in the central West Bank.
Municipal chief Marwan Sabah told AA that a group of occupiers stormed the village around midnight and set three vehicles ablaze.
"Confrontations broke out between residents and the attackers, forcing the occupiers to withdraw," he said.
"Umm Safa has repeatedly come under attack by Israeli occupiers involving assaults on residents, vehicle arson, intimidation and harassment," Sabah said.
He added that occupiers have seized large areas of the village’s land.
Israeli occupiers also established a settlement outpost at the northern entrance to al-Bireh overlooking the al-Balou neighborhood, the Bedouin rights group al-Baidar said.
According to the Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission, Israeli occupiers attempted to establish 21 new settlement outposts across the West Bank in September, including 10 in Ramallah and al-Bireh governorate.
The incidents come amid intensified Israeli army raids and attacks by Israeli occupiers against Palestinians across the occupied West Bank since the start of Israel’s war on Gaza in October 2023.

For its nominee to lead the UN would be an outrage | Nesrine Malik  The GuardianIsrael’s Danon Praises UAE’s Nusseibeh But Stops Short Of Backing Her UN Bid  i24NEWSWho is Lana Nusseibeh, the UAE diplomat hoping to become the ne...
articles.full_text:
The United Kingdom is leaning towards backing Emirati diplomat Lana Nusseibeh as secretary-general of the United Nations, Middle East Eye can reveal.
Nusseibeh's candidacy has drawn controversy over the United Arab Emirates' role in Sudan’s civil war, where it is accused of supporting the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, whose mass killings UN investigators say bear the “hallmarks of genocide”. The UAE denies the allegations.
Her candidacy has also drawn criticism over the UAE's close ties with Israel.
Numerous sources close to the British government told Middle East Eye the UK - a permanent member of the UN - is leaning towards supporting Nusseibeh's candidacy for the role, although a final decision has not yet been made.
A British Foreign Office spokesperson told MEE: "The UK’s priority is to find the candidate best equipped to lead the UN in tackling our shared global challenges.
"Our focus is on the merit of the candidates to secure the most qualified candidate for the next UN secretary-general. We will not be publicly commenting on individual candidates."
The UK supporting Nusseibeh could be perceived as smoothening Prime Minister Andy Burnham's relationship with Abu Dhabi after a major row in Britain over Manchester City Football Club, owned by Emirati royal and vice-president Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nayhan.
The club was found last month to have breached 114 Premier League financial rules by disguising more than £830m ($1.1bn) in illicit funding.
Manchester City denies the claims and Emirati officials have since reportedly threatened to cancel investments in Britain over "the Premier League’s actions".
Multiple sources said that if the UK backs Nusseibeh as UN secretary-general, it might win the country some goodwill with the UAE at a time when relations are fraught.
If selected Nusseibeh, 48, would be the first woman to lead the UN and its second Arab secretary-general, after Egypt's Boutros Boutros-Ghali.
Her entry into the race last week followed six informal straw polls in which no candidate secured the backing of the five veto-wielding permanent members of the UN: Britain, the US, Russia, China and France.
The current secretary-general, Antonio Guterres, will end his term in December. The council must agree a candidate for the 193-member General Assembly to approve, but it remains unclear whether it will do so before then.
Controversial record
Born in 1978, Nusseibeh worked as a Unesco consultant and an analyst at the Gulf Research Centre before becoming founding director of the UAE foreign ministry's policy planning department.
She became the UAE's first female permanent representative to the UN in 2013 and served until 2024, during which time she was a vice-president of the General Assembly, president of the UN Women executive board and twice president of the Security Council.
Nusseibeh is of Palestinian heritage and her family hails from Jerusalem. Her grandfather, Anwar Nusseibeh, was a prominent Palestinian politician who held ministerial posts in Jordan's government when it controlled the West Bank and East Jerusalem, and served as Jordan's ambassador to Britain.
Colin Shindler, an emeritus professor of Israeli studies at Soas who taught her when she was a student at that university, wrote in a 2020 Jewish Chronicle column that she had completed a master's in Israeli studies.
He said she'd wrote some "wonderfully insightful and incisive essays on Zionism and Israeli history", and described her as "instrumental" in the normalisation deal, known as the Abraham Accords.
In September 2025, as Israel weighed annexing parts of the occupied West Bank, Nusseibeh said the UAE had always seen the accords as a way to support Palestinians and urged the Israeli government to suspend its plans.
"I am standing to be secretary-general because I believe this is a moment to act with greater urgency: to act earlier, bring people together across difference, and drive the work forward until it produces concrete results," she said in a statement launching her campaign last week.
Sudan atrocities
On Monday, the UK announced it was sanctioning 15 senior commanders from both the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) in Sudan for "suspected atrocities, including conflict-related sexual violence".
This comes a year after the RSF massacred civilians in Sudan's Al Fasher. British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said: "A year on from the atrocities in El Fasher, UK-funded investigations have shown that rape and starvation are still being weaponised against the people of Sudan.
"These are crimes against our humanity - the perpetrators must be held accountable and support from all external backers to the warring parties must end."
UN experts and rights groups have concluded in several authoritative reports that the RSF has committed genocide and other international crimes against non-Arab communities in Darfur.
There is widespread public evidence, including extensive reporting by MEE, linking the UAE with the supply of arms and other goods to the RSF, although the Emirati government, including Nusseibeh, have repeatedly denied this.

articles.title: Saudi-led coalition says it destroyed Houthi missile facilities, and other Mideast news - Delco Times
articles.summary: Saudi-led coalition says it destroyed Houthi missile facilities, and other Mideast news  Delco Times
articles.full_text:
By The Associated Press
The Saudi-led coalition battling Yemen’s Houthi rebels said Monday that it has degraded their ability to strike targets inside the kingdom after destroying tunnels used to store ballistic missiles and missile launchers.
In Israel, the country’s defense minister strongly denied that the military has clashed with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu over his reported instructions for an “action” against Iran ahead of national elections on Tuesday.
Here is the latest news from the Middle East on Monday. Read our full coverage here.
Saudi-led coalition says it destroyed Houthi missile launchers
An operation in Houthi-controlled territory in Yemen destroyed five tunnels used for storing ballistic missiles, four ballistic missile launchers and another missile storage facility, according to the spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Iran-backed Houthis.
Maj. Gen. Turki al-Malki said the operation also aimed to cut the Houthis’ supply lines between areas under their control and targeted rebel fortifications and military equipment along the front lines inside Yemen.
In a post on X, al-Malki said the coalition would continue to use “deterrent operational measures” to protect against the Houthis’ “brutal attacks” inside the kingdom and in Yemen.
Houthis say Saudi-backed forces struck hospital in Red Sea port city
Yemen’s Houthi-run Health Ministry said Monday that Saudi-backed forces targeted a hospital in the Red Sea port city of Mokha, which the Houthi rebels recently seized. It did not provide evidence for the claim, and The Associated Press could not independently verify it.
In a statement, the ministry said the attack caused extensive damage to the hospital, but did not say whether there were any casualties. It also said Saudi forces on Sunday targeted a children’s hospital in Taiz province, causing damage.
Earlier on Monday, two residents of Mokha, who spoke on condition of anonymity for fear of reprisals, said Mokha General Hospital and at least 10 houses were damaged after a rocket struck a nearby four-story residential building. The AP could not independently verify the claim, and it was not clear if this was the same incident that the Health Ministry was referring to.
There was no immediate comment from the Saudi-backed forces.
— By Ahmed al-Haj in Aden, Yemen
Houthis say they fired missiles at Yemeni government forces
The Houthi rebels claimed Monday that they struck military gatherings and weapons depots belonging to Saudi-backed government forces in Aden and Lahj provinces.
The Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said in a statement that the rebels fired ballistic missiles at the sites, inflicting losses. The claims could not be independently verified.
The Houthis continue to target government forces and their allies inside Yemen. The Yemeni government accused the rebels on Sunday of targeting displacement camps on the outskirts of the southern port city of Aden. The government didn’t provide evidence to support its claim.
Israel’s defense minister denies clash with the army over Iran
Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz on Monday dismissed reports regarding rifts between the political leadership and the Israeli military over Iran as “completely baseless and false.”
In a post on X, Katz also said Israel had no intention to strike Iran before Tuesday’s national elections but that it would respond “with great force” if Iran attacks first.
Israeli Channel 12 reported Sunday evening that Benjamin Netanyahu and Israel’s military chief of staff clashed over the Israeli prime minister’s instruction to carry out an “action” that the army believes could quickly reignite the conflict with Iran. The report did not specify the nature of the action. Netanyahu’s office later described the report as “fake news.”
Iran, Saudi Arabia, Turkey, Pakistan seek closer cooperation
Iran, Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan agreed Monday to continue talks on strengthening cooperation, particularly on regional peace and security, Iran’s state-run news agency IRNA reported.
Maj. Gen. Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, hosted the four countries’ first quadrilateral meeting in Tehran.
Saudi Defense Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman, Pakistan’s armed forces chief Gen. Asim Munir and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin attended.
The IRNA report did not specify when or where the next meeting would take place.
Meanwhile, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan said renewed attacks on Iran would destabilize the region and hurt countries that are not party to the conflict. In a televised address on Monday, he said reports about potential attacks had already driven fuel prices higher.
UN chief ‘alarmed’ by Israeli settler violence
U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres said Monday he was “deeply alarmed” by surging Israeli settler violence and settlement expansion in the West Bank.
Speaking in Cairo on one of his final trips as U.N. chief, Guterres called for lifting Israeli restrictions on humanitarian aid to Gaza and removing obstacles to the Security Council’s peace plan, warning that “the specter of ethnic cleansing” was looming ever larger.
He said lasting peace in the region depends on Palestinians’ right to self-determination and that a two-state solution, with Jerusalem as the capital of both states, is the only viable path.
Guterres also called for restoring stability around Iran and the Strait of Hormuz and ensuring safety around Yemen’s Bab al-Mandeb Strait.
Egypt’s parliament approves help to Saudi Arabia
Egyptian lawmakers on Monday approved President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi’s request to support Saudi Arabia in countering Houthi attacks.
The decision comes amid growing public concern that Egypt could become involved in Yemen’s long-running conflict.
Egypt’s highest security body had pledged to provide “all necessary and possible forms of support” to Saudi Arabia to defend its security and stability, protect its resources and territorial integrity, and safeguard Islamic holy sites.
