articles.title: The Geopolitics of Trade Infrastructure - Middle East Institute
articles.summary: The Geopolitics of Trade Infrastructure  Middle East Institute
articles.full_text:
On March 1, 2026, debris from an intercepted aerial object ignited a fire at a berth in Jebel Ali, the Middle East’s largest container port. Port operator DP World temporarily suspended terminal operations, while Mediterranean Shipping Company (MSC) halted new bookings for regional cargo. Iranian drone strikes also damaged Amazon Web Services (AWS) facilities in the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain, disrupting cloud services used by financial institutions and commercial platforms. Together, these incidents exposed a vulnerability in global commerce: its dependence on interconnected infrastructure spanning multiple jurisdictions.
Ports, for example, rely on terminal software, communications networks, cloud computing, and satellite navigation, as well as physical facilities. Disruption to any one of these systems can cascade across the wider trading network.
Geopolitical influence over trade increasingly rests on controlling the systems that make them work. The Middle East illustrates the stakes. US ports, cable corridors, cloud facilities, artificial intelligence (AI) investments, and maritime routes connect regional economies to global commerce while exposing them to external decisions and disruptions. For the United States, the challenge is to translate technological advantage into resilient networks rather than rely on centrality that can itself become a source of vulnerability and coercion.
From Ports to Digital Infrastructure
Modern ports depend on software and shared data to coordinate vessel arrivals, cargo handling, berth allocation, and customs clearance. Digital coordination can make port calls more predictable, but it also creates dependencies among terminal operators, shipping lines, and public authorities.
Terminal ownership and software provision are distinct. COSCO Shipping Ports, a Chinese state-owned operator, has subscribed to Navis terminal operating software, from the US supply chain software provider Kaleris, for hundreds of berths across dozens of ports. The arrangement illustrates how the operator of a physical facility may rely on a foreign supplier for the systems that organize daily operations. In Morocco, Eurogate Tanger replaced Navis with a Korean-made system in 2021, demonstrating that alternatives exist but also that changing systems requires time, money, and operational adjustment.
These dependencies matter even when no adversary deliberately intervenes. A software failure, loss of connectivity, or restriction on access can slow cargo handling and disrupt schedules. Physical damage can produce similar effects, as the Jebel Ali incident showed. The strategic question is therefore not only who owns a port but who can keep it operating when the systems beneath it fail.
The Digital Arteries of Trade
Submarine cables carry most intercontinental data traffic. Their routes are therefore critical to commerce, finance, communications, and public services. Egypt is a major chokepoint between Europe, Asia, and Africa, while its position gives local authorities and cable operators an important role in access and repair. Concentration along a limited number of routes means that damage can affect users far from the point of failure.
In September 2025, cuts to three cables near Jeddah disrupted connectivity across parts of the Middle East and Asia, prompting Microsoft to warn Azure customers of increased latency. The cause was considered likely to be commercial shipping activity rather than deliberate sabotage. That distinction matters: infrastructure can be vulnerable without being targeted. Redundancy helps, but traffic can only be rerouted if spare capacity exists. Repairs depend on specialized vessels, favorable conditions, and permits; delays can prolong the disruption. Insecurity around Bab al-Mandab adds another risk, while proposed overland alternatives remain incomplete.
The relevant measure of resilience is not simply the number of cables or routes available. It is how quickly alternatives can absorb disrupted traffic, and whether operators can restore service before commercial consequences compound.
Cloud, Chips, and the Gulf
Saudi Arabia and the UAE are investing heavily in data centers and AI to diversify their economies. Yet investment does not automatically deliver technological autonomy. Advanced AI depends on specialized chips, computing platforms, software, and expertise that Gulf states cannot yet supply entirely on their own.
The UAE’s partnership with Microsoft and AI and cloud computing firm G42 illustrates both the opportunity and the dependence. Microsoft has announced major investment in the country, including a stake in G42. In November 2025, US authorities authorized exports of advanced computing chips to G42 and Saudi Arabian AI company HUMAIN, subject to security and reporting requirements. Those approvals followed G42’s break with restricted Chinese technology corporation Huawei and HUMAIN’s pledge not to purchase its equipment. The decisions show how Washington’s control over advanced technology can influence the pace and terms of Gulf AI development.
That leverage was reinforced, but recalibrated, by a July 2026 Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) rule moving the UAE into Country Group A:5, which eases access to certain controlled technologies and allows approved entities to receive specified advanced computing items without individual licenses. License requirements for those items remain for any recipient not on the approved list.
These partnerships bring capital, expertise, and access to computing power. They also give foreign suppliers — and the governments that regulate them — a role in determining what can be built and how quickly. Other suppliers are available, but technologies are not always interchangeable. Switching providers can require costly changes to software, data management, security arrangements, and staff expertise.
The risk is not dependence in itself. It is dependence without credible alternatives or plans for continuity. Concentrated cloud services can become a single point of failure for banking, logistics, government services, and the commercial platforms on which everyday activity increasingly relies.
When the Cloud Becomes a Target
The March 2026 strikes on AWS facilities in the UAE and Bahrain underscored the physical exposure of digital infrastructure. Damage to data centers disrupted services used by banks and commercial platforms, demonstrating that a facility built to support routine economic activity can become a target during regional conflict. The consequences extended beyond the sites themselves because businesses rely on cloud platforms to manage inventories, process payments, coordinate shipping, and track goods. As of mid-September, more than six months on from the strikes, service to the AWS facilities had still not been restored.
The vulnerability is systemic. Cable damage can impair connectivity; attacks on data centers can interrupt computing services; and restrictions on access to advanced chips can constrain the development or replacement of systems. These layers reinforce one another. A backup cloud provider offers limited protection if it depends on the same vulnerable cable, power supply, or geographic corridor. The Gulf region is particularly exposed, with more than 90% of data capacity from Europe to Asia passing through the Red Sea. Its vulnerability was underscored once again in mid-October, when Iran threatened to target submarine cables, data centers, and AI facilities across the region if the war with the US resumed.
Governments face a related tension between resilience and data localization. Keeping data inside national borders may serve legitimate regulatory and security goals, but geographic concentration can leave services exposed to a single conflict or natural disaster. Distributing workloads across locations can improve continuity, provided governments and operators establish clear rules for data protection, access, and emergency recovery. The goal should not be to abandon local infrastructure, but to avoid designing systems whose essential functions can be disabled by one localized event.
Satellite Navigation and Positional Dependence
Satellite navigation supplies the positional and timing information that helps coordinate ships, aircraft, vehicles, port equipment, and telecommunications networks. The United States’ Global Positioning System (GPS), Europe’s Galileo, Russia’s Global Navigation Satellite System (GLONASS), and China’s BeiDou support civilian and commercial users both inside and outside their home jurisdictions. Their importance extends beyond telling a vessel where it is: navigation and timing services help synchronize activities across physical and digital infrastructure.
Unlike a port or cable, satellite navigation can be disrupted without damaging the underlying system. Jamming overwhelms legitimate signals; spoofing deceives receivers with false position or timing information. In March 2026, maritime advisories reported GPS spoofing in the Persian Gulf, the Strait of Hormuz, and the Gulf of Oman, warning mariners to verify satellite data independently.
The effects can spread beyond an individual vessel. Inaccurate positioning can distort tracking displays, complicate traffic management, increase collision risks, and disrupt port approaches. Access to multiple satellite constellations does not guarantee resilience if receivers, procedures, or supporting systems share vulnerabilities. Nor can alternative signals alone solve interference affecting several systems in the same area.
Resilience therefore requires layered safeguards: multi-constellation receivers, terrestrial and inertial navigation alternatives, radar and visual verification, and procedures for operating when satellite signals become unreliable. articles.title: AI data centre growth hits ESG and infrastructure limits - MEED
articles.summary: AI data centre growth hits ESG and infrastructure limits  MEED
articles.full_text:
Data centre growth driven by demand for artificial intelligence (AI) is colliding with environmental, social and governance (ESG) and infrastructure constraints.
Annual data centre power consumption is expected to rise from 590 terawatt-hours (TWh) in 2025 to 1,520TWh in 2030, accounting for 4.5% of global electricity consumption, up from 2.1% in 2025. However, rising water use in already water-stressed areas, growing public opposition, grid connection delays and shortages of materials and skilled labour are delaying data centre projects and could slow AI progress, according to UK analytics firm GlobalData.
GlobalData’s latest Strategic Intelligence report, The Constraints Reshaping Data Centre Development, reveals that most announced data centre projects remain stuck in the planning stage. Projects that broke ground between the third quarter of 2025 and Q3 2026 waited an average of just over two years from announcement to the start of construction, up from about 18 months for those that started between Q1 2020 and Q2 2025.
Martina Raveni, senior analyst, Strategic Intelligence team at GlobalData, comments: “Data centres are increasingly located in water-stressed areas, and their construction, along with the energy-intensive training and running of large language models, is adding new sources of emissions. Together with concerns over noise, land use and rising electricity bills, these impacts are hardening public opposition. According to Data Centre Watch, in Q1 2026 alone, at least 75 US data centre projects worth roughly $130bn were blocked or delayed, the largest single-quarter total on record. Similar backlash is emerging in countries including the UK, Chile, South Korea and Japan.”
Grid access has become a major bottleneck. According to the International Energy Agency's 2026 Electricity Outlook, more than 2,500GW of renewable, large-load and storage projects are waiting in connection queues worldwide, and developers in Europe’s main data centre hubs can face waits of 7-10 years. Building new grid infrastructure can take 5-15 years, compared to the 1-3 years required to build a data centre. Grid congestion is pushing operators towards on-site gas power, which risks increasing emissions even as grids decarbonise.
Raveni continues: “Data centre buildout also depends on fragile supply chains. A single hyperscale facility can require up to 50,000 tons of copper, while AI data centres need 10-20 times more fibre than traditional builds, at a time when fibre manufacturers are already at capacity. On top of this, a shortage of electricians and other skilled trades is delaying projects.”
The industry is responding on several fronts, although progress remains uneven. Operators are adopting closed-loop cooling; expanding water stewardship commitments; diversifying their power supplies through renewables, battery storage and fuel cells; and extending equipment lifespans through circular economy practices. Community engagement and workforce development are increasingly treated as core requirements for project delivery.
Raveni concludes: “These constraints are already translating into real delays for AI infrastructure. As capacity tightens, compute becomes more expensive and harder to access, pushing AI developers towards smaller models and more limited use cases. Unless grid access, equipment supplies and construction timelines become more predictable, AI progress will be shaped as much by power and hardware logistics as by algorithmic innovation.”

articles.title: Israel exit polls show opposition edge, Arab parties make gains
articles.summary: Israeli opposition parties appeared to hold a slim lead over Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc in Tuesday's general election, according to initial exit polls, as a surge in...
articles.full_text:
Israeli opposition parties appeared to hold a slim lead over Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc in Tuesday's general election, according to initial exit polls, as a surge in Arab voter turnout put Arab-majority parties on course for significant parliamentary gains.
Early projections broadcast by Israeli television networks showed that the bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot, a center-right former military chief, had a narrow edge over Netanyahu's bloc, which includes the far-right.
Israeli Arab parties made sweeping gains, likely giving them a critical role in the next parliament, the early exit polls showed.
With no single party winning the majority, Israeli politicians will embark on potentially weeks of high-stakes negotiations on cobbling together a coalition.
The country's main pollsters – Channels 11, 12 and 13 – projected the opposition bloc to win 52 to 53 seats, and Netanyahu's bloc to win around 50, although his Likud would be the largest single party in the parliament, with 24 or 25 seats.
In a dash to secure as many votes as possible, Netanyahu had charged that Israeli Arabs were out to "steal the election" and his Likud party unsuccessfully asked election authorities to keep polls open past 10:00 p.m. (2000 GMT).
His efforts led the opposition to charge that he was looking for pretexts to challenge the results.
"We cannot leave this battle here in the hands of the left and the Arab parties that want to bring an end to the Jewish state," a visibly tense Netanyahu told supporters as he tried to bring up turnout in a Likud stronghold.
Nationwide turnout as of 8:00 p.m. stood at nearly 75%, the highest in decades.
Israelis cast their ballots in the shadow of Oct. 7 and the multi-front regional wars that it sparked, with the trauma from the attack still fresh and questions over accountability and security central to the campaign.
The close-fought vote comes as Israel looks increasingly isolated on the world stage, driven by the war in Iran and the genocidal military attacks in Gaza, soaring settlement construction and violence in the occupied West Bank.
Netanyahu himself faces an arrest warrant from the International Criminal Court over Gaza genocide, as well as domestic corruption charges that could land him in prison.
Eisenkot, his main rival, is a political novice and former military chief whose mild manner is seen as the antithesis of the incumbent.
Speaking afterwards at a polling station, Eisenkot called on Israelis to vote to replace "the worst government since the state was established."
Some 7.3 million people were eligible to vote, with tens of thousands of Israelis estimated to have flown in from abroad for an election seen as crucial to deciding the future character of their country.
Eilana Zisblit, 55, told AFP she had travelled back from Canada, where she has lived for almost 30 years, to vote for a center-right party in Eisenkot's bloc.
"The country is going in a really, really bad direction. Both for Jews and Arabs living in the country, and for Jews living abroad," she said.
The time to act is "now, or the country really won't survive anymore".
Netanyahu, 77, has served as prime minister on and off for more than 19 years.
Throughout his career, he has repeatedly raised the spectre of Arab voters as a threat. He warned Tuesday of Arabs voting by the busload, writing on social media that Israel could wake up to a "government of the left wing and Muslim Brotherhood."
The acting director general of the Central Elections Committee, Dean Livne, said that police had "caught individuals who tried to bribe voters", adding that the unidentified suspects were not at polling stations and were caught near their homes.
He said the matter was a localised case and under investigation.
United Arab List head Mansour Abbas, who could emerge as a kingmaker in a close election, accused Netanyahu of "lying and inciting" to mobilize his voters.
Exit polls from the main Israeli television channels showed the two Arab lists winning 17 or 18 seats in the 120-member parliament between them, up from 10 in the last election in 2022.
In Tel Aviv, left-wing party The Democrats, which is part of Eisenkot's opposition bloc, said police had arrested a man with a knife who had moved threateningly towards its leader Yair Golan.
"Incitement and violence will not intimidate us," Golan said in a statement, blaming the incident on the "poison machine" of Netanyahu.
Netanyahu last returned to power in December 2022, bringing into his coalition far-right ultra-nationalists who have since seen their political clout skyrocket and have aggressively championed settlements in the West Bank.
In the last days of the campaign, he posted an image of a nuclear bomb destroying Tel Aviv and talked up his endorsement by US President Donald Trump, who is also fond of alleging election fraud.

articles.title: Highest half-day voter turnout on record marks key Israel election
articles.summary: Turnout in Tuesday's Israeli election, seen as a referendum on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, was at the highest level on record at the midway point, the Central Elections Comm...
articles.full_text:
Turnout in Tuesday's Israeli election, seen as a referendum on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, was at the highest level on record at the midway point, the Central Elections Commission said.
As of 2 p.m. (1200 GMT), 3.29 million Israelis, or 44.9% of eligible voters, had cast a ballot, the highest turnout since the commission started recording such statistics in 1973, its head Dean Livne said.
"We have broken all records registered by the Elections Committee since 1973," Livneh said. "There has been no such data."
Earlier, the Elections Committee said a total of 2.39 million Israelis had cast their ballots by noon local time (10 a.m. GMT), an increase of more than 3 percentage points compared with the previous election.
Extremist Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich attributed the high turnout to exceptionally strong participation among Arab voters and in left-wing strongholds.
More than 7.3 million Israelis are eligible to vote in Tuesday's elections to choose members of the 120-seat Knesset.
Polling stations opened at 7 a.m. local time (0500 GMT) and are scheduled to close at 10 p.m. (2000 GMT).
The elections are Israel's first general polls since the start of its genocidal war in the Gaza Strip in October 2023.

articles.title: Israelis flock to polls to pass wartime judgment on Netanyahu
articles.summary: Israelis voted Tuesday at the highest rate in 45 years, delivering a wartime verdict on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in what many called the nation's most consequential electi...
articles.full_text:
Israelis voted Tuesday at the highest rate in 45 years, delivering a wartime verdict on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in what many called the nation's most consequential election.
Voters will go to polls for the first election since the Oct. 7, 2023 Hamas incursion and Israel's consequent genocidal war on Gaza, as well as in Lebanon and Iran.
Policies of Netanyahu's right-wing coalition have been divisive at home and have deepened Israel's international isolation, but he has defended his record as the only leader with the mettle to face Israel's foes.
Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving leader with 19 years in office, is an unmatched political survivor and his nationalist politics are increasingly entrenched.
Israel's fragmented system makes it difficult for an array of opponents to force out his coalition of right-wing, far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties.
His main rival Gadi Eisenkot, a military ex-chief of staff and security hawk, aims to unseat him with the support of parties on the right and center, as well as the rump of an increasingly marginalized left. Opinion polls show a close race, with neither leader facing an easy path to power.
Voters began casting ballots after polling stations opened at 7 a.m. (5 a.m. GMT). The polls close at 10 p.m. (8 p.m. GMT).
The Central Elections Committee reported that 16.7% of eligible voters had already cast their ballots within the first three hours, the fastest early turnout rate since 1981.
"I think these elections are the most important of all the ones I’ve known," said Ruth Epstein, an 81-year-old longtime left-wing voter in Ramat Gan near Tel Aviv, who voted for the opposition Democrats.
"I’m really scared about what will be here."
Netanyahu supporter Louis Lipsky of Jerusalem said he was voting to keep the prime minister in power, crediting him with normalizing relations with several Arab states under the Abraham Accords of 2020.
Netanyahu has campaigned on his wartime leadership and an endorsement from U.S. President Donald Trump, his ally in war against Iran, who has said they should "finish the job."
If neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot can form a governing coalition in the 120-seat parliament, Netanyahu could stay on as caretaker until another election is held.
His opponents have managed to wrest him from the premiership only once since 2009, and that took four inconclusive elections in two years. He was back 18 months later.
For many of Netanyahu's opponents, the election turns on accountability for the security failures of Oct. 7. Opposition groups have promised to hold a national inquiry, which Netanyahu's government has resisted.
"I am convinced that by the end of today, we will see a change – a new spirit for the State of Israel – that will serve as a rectification for the past three years and for that terrible day," Eisenkot said during a visit to kibbutz Nir Oz in southern Israel.
He walked to the polls with Gadi Mozes, one of 251 people kidnapped by Hamas and taken to Gaza during the Oct. 7 attack that caused 1,200 deaths.
Eisenkot says Israel's response – a genocidal war which health authorities say killed more than 74,000 Palestinians – was a failure because Hamas remains in charge. International community and U.N.-commissioned experts agree the Israel committed "genocide" against the Palestinians living in Gaza.
He repeated his commitment to dismantle Hamas' military and governing power in Gaza within 18 months of forming a government.
In his first public commentary on election day, Netanyahu shared an article on X about an incident in which police said three people were arrested over an election bribery attempt.
"Right-wing voters, dear Likud voters, in the face of attempts to undermine the integrity of the elections, we must go out and vote en masse, vote Likud for the sake of our country," he said.
Netanyahu's critics have said the prime minister may try to cast doubt on the integrity of the voting process, which his office rejects.
Itamar Ben-Gvir, leader of a far-right party in Netanyahu's coalition, cast his vote in the Kiryat Arba settlement in the occupied West Bank early Tuesday. He predicted Netanyahu would return as prime minister and his own party would serve as the right-wing anchor of the government.
Voters from Israel's Arab minority – Israeli by citizenship but Palestinian by heritage – were voting in "unprecedented" numbers, Palestinian candidate Ahmed Tibi said.
Eisenkot has ruled out partnering with Arab parties, citing a lack of shared values, although some experts envision them propping up a minority government to ensure Netanyahu is removed from office.
"My expectation is that we will have only a slight majority either way. No landslide," said Israeli political analyst Amotz Asa-El of the Shalom Hartman Institute.
Eisenkot joined Netanyahu's war cabinet after the Oct. 7 incursion but quit after eight months, criticizing his leadership.
Israel flattened much of Gaza in the genocidal war after Oct. 7 and now occupies around two-thirds of the enclave under a year-old U.S.-brokered cease-fire.
Israel also dealt heavy blows to Iran-backed Hezbollah in Lebanon and traded strikes with Iran, culminating in a 12-day aerial campaign against Iranian nuclear sites in 2025 and this year's joint U.S.-Israeli war.
Like nearly all Jewish-led parties in Israel, Eisenkot opposes the two-state solution that underpinned decades of peace negotiations with the Palestinians.
But he has criticized illegal Jewish settler violence against Palestinians in the Israeli-occupied West Bank, which has surged since 2023 and strained Israel's ties with Western states. And he opposes Netanyahu's far-right coalition partners.

articles.title: Israeli election: 4 scenarios facing country's next government
articles.summary: Israel faces four potential scenarios for government formation if neither Benjamin Netanyahu nor Gadi Eisenkot secures a majority in Tuesday’s general election, according to an Isr...
articles.full_text:
Israel faces four potential scenarios for government formation if neither Benjamin Netanyahu nor Gadi Eisenkot secures a majority in Tuesday’s general election, according to an Israeli politics expert.
Opinion polls suggest that neither Netanyahu’s Likud party nor Eisenkot’s Yashar party is expected to lead a bloc capable of securing the 61 seats needed for a majority in the 120-member Knesset, Israel’s parliament.
Israel uses a nationwide proportional representation system in which voters cast ballots for party lists rather than individual candidates. The prime minister is not directly elected but must be able to secure the confidence of at least 61 lawmakers.
As no single party typically wins a parliamentary majority, governments are generally formed through coalitions of parties with broadly compatible political positions.
Wadie Abu Nassar, an expert on Israeli politics, outlined four possible scenarios in comments to Anadolu Agency (AA).
“The first scenario is that Netanyahu or Eisenkot manages to form a regular government through a coalition with parties that win seats in the polls,” Abu Nassar said.
He described that outcome as difficult, given polling projections that neither Netanyahu’s bloc nor the opposition camp would secure the required majority.
“Still, this scenario cannot be completely ruled out, particularly amid reports that Eisenkot is trying to win over lawmakers from the Haredi parties to support a government he would form,” he added.
The second scenario would involve Eisenkot forming a minority government backed by Arab lawmakers who would support it in parliament without joining the governing coalition, Abu Nassar said.
Arab parties in Israel have said they could provide Eisenkot with a parliamentary “safety net” in exchange for guarantees addressing the concerns of Arab citizens.
The arrangement would aim to prevent the current government, which includes far-right ministers Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, from remaining in office as a caretaker administration.
The Joint List, an alliance of three Arab parties led by Yousef Jabareen, and the United Arab List, headed by Mansour Abbas, have expressed willingness to support an Eisenkot-led government from outside the coalition.
Their demands include halting home demolitions, combating crime in Arab communities and opening a political horizon with the Palestinians.
Eisenkot has not taken a definitive position on the proposal, although he has previously ruled out including Arab parties in a coalition he seeks to form.
Polls suggest that 13 party lists could enter the Knesset, including two representing Arab citizens, who account for about 20% of Israel’s population of more than 10 million.
Opinion polls project that the Arab parties could win a combined 14 to 15 seats.
The third scenario would involve a national unity government bringing together Netanyahu, Eisenkot and other parties, Abu Nassar said.
“There are discussions in Israeli circles that if the elections reach a deadlock, meaning neither bloc obtains the required majority to form a government, a national unity government could be formed,” he said.
Abu Nassar said Israeli President Isaac Herzog has been pushing for such an arrangement to avoid another election. Reports also indicate that figures close to U.S. President Donald Trump favor the option.
Under the proposed arrangement, Likud and Yashar would join other parties in a government led by Netanyahu and Eisenkot, while Ben-Gvir’s Jewish Power party and Smotrich’s Religious Zionism party would be excluded, Abu Nassar said.
The main obstacle is opposition parties’ refusal to join a government with Netanyahu or one led by him, Abu Nassar said. Netanyahu, however, appears open to a unity government in which he and Eisenkot would rotate as prime minister, provided Netanyahu serves first.
“Opposition parties do not necessarily reject joining Likud in a unity government but object to Netanyahu personally,” Abu Nassar said.
Some Israeli political circles have raised the possibility of Herzog granting Netanyahu a pardon in his corruption cases in exchange for his withdrawal from political life, Abu Nassar added.
Netanyahu has said he would not leave politics even if he loses the election.
He faces charges of bribery, fraud and breach of trust in three separate cases, known as Cases 1000, 2000 and 4000. He denies wrongdoing.
Separately, the International Criminal Court (ICC) issued an arrest warrant for Netanyahu on Nov. 21, 2024, over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza.
More than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed by Israel’s genocidal military offensive in Gaza since October 2023, according to figures cited in the original report.
Ben-Gvir has also claimed that Netanyahu has avoided appearing in photographs with him because he is pursuing a possible unity government with Eisenkot.
The fourth scenario would involve neither Netanyahu nor the opposition succeeding in forming a government, leaving the current Cabinet in place as a caretaker administration until another election could be held several months later.
“In the fourth scenario, elections would be repeated after several months, and until then the current government would remain as a caretaker government until a new one is formed,” Abu Nassar said.
“This is the scenario Netanyahu would prefer and work toward if he fails to form a government,” he added.
Under Israeli law, Knesset elections are normally held every four years, although an election can be called earlier if the political system fails to produce a functioning government or other legal conditions for an early vote are met.
The election is widely seen as crucial to Netanyahu’s political future. The 76-year-old prime minister is standing trial in Iarael on charges including bribery, fraud and breach of trust. A conviction could result in imprisonment.
Netanyahu is also subject to an ICC arrest warrant issued in 2024 over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza during Israel’s genocidal military campaign since October 2023.

articles.title: Brazil's Flavio Bolsonaro leaves for US after election defeat
articles.summary: Brazilian Sen. Flavio Bolsonaro has traveled to the United States following his defeat in Sunday's presidential election, defying a Supreme Court order requiring him to surrender h...
articles.full_text:
Brazilian Sen. Flavio Bolsonaro has traveled to the United States following his defeat in Sunday's presidential election, defying a Supreme Court order requiring him to surrender his passports, two sources said.
The U.S. Embassy in Brazil did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Bolsonaro's lawyer also did not respond.
It was not immediately clear where Bolsonaro was heading, what time he would arrive or whether he would seek asylum. U.S. President Donald Trump's administration has previously alleged Flavio's father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, was a victim of judicial persecution in Brazil.
Flavio's departure for the United States threatens to deepen a rift between the two most populous nations in the Americas. President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva has accused Washington of colluding with the Bolsonaros to put them back in power, and Reuters reported ahead of Sunday's election on a U.S. State Department campaign to restore them to office.
Lula's office did not respond to a request for comment.
Bolsonaro was favored to win Sunday's presidential election but ended up losing in a shock result to leftist Lula.
On Monday, he was given 24 hours to surrender his passports as part of a money laundering probe in which he denies wrongdoing, but that deadline has now lapsed, two other sources said, leading to his documents being canceled.
Bolsonaro, who loses his immunity from prosecution when his Senate term ends in February, said on Monday he had no plans to flee.
"I have never thought about leaving the country," he said. "I will hand over my passports and defend myself against this travesty, which is a clear attempt to intimidate me."
Jair Bolsonaro also went to the United States after refusing to concede to Lula in 2022, when former U.S. President Joe Biden was in office. He eventually returned to Brazil but was later given a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup after his supporters stormed government buildings in Brasilia.
His son has yet to officially concede defeat - saying on Sunday he would seek the annulment of the result over alleged voter irregularities - but his Liberal Party said on Monday it acknowledged Lula's victory.
It remains unclear how Bolsonaro was able to leave the country while he was facing a 24-hour deadline to hand over his passports. A senior Federal Police official said Bolsonaro had not exited the country via any regular migration point.
Eduardo Bolsonaro, Bolsonaro's younger brother who lives in the United States, said ahead of the vote that an election loss would require a move.
"If my brother does not win, I'm in favor that he would leave the country," he told podcaster Steven Crowder this month.

articles.title: Pakistan Embassy in Ankara calls for Kashmir peace, dialogue
articles.summary: Pakistan's Embassy in Ankara called for renewed diplomatic efforts to resolve the long-standing Kashmir dispute, emphasizing justice, regional stability and the rights of Kashmiri...
articles.full_text:
Pakistan's Embassy in Ankara called for renewed diplomatic efforts to resolve the long-standing Kashmir dispute, emphasizing justice, regional stability and the rights of Kashmiri people during a panel discussion held Tuesday to mark Kashmir Black Day.
The event, organized in cooperation with the Strategic Thinking Institute (SDE), commemorated the arrival of Indian troops in Srinagar on Oct. 27, 1947, a date observed by Pakistan as Kashmir Black Day.
Titled "The Jammu and Kashmir Issue in the 79th Year of Occupation," the panel brought together diplomats, historians and researchers to examine the dispute's historical, political and humanitarian dimensions.
Pakistan's chargé d'affaires in Ankara, Shaiq Ahmed Bhutto, said lasting peace in Kashmir required justice, political legitimacy and meaningful participation by the Kashmiri people.
Referring to relevant U.N. Security Council resolutions, Bhutto reiterated Pakistan's commitment to resolving the dispute peacefully in accordance with international law and the wishes of Kashmiris.
He also emphasized the need to protect human dignity, ease regional tensions and promote dialogue, while expressing appreciation for Türkiye's continued support for a peaceful settlement.
Former Consul General in Karachi Cemal Sangu addressed the dispute's historical background and implications for regional security, highlighting humanitarian challenges facing Kashmiris.
Sangu called for maintaining the cease-fire, reviving dialogue between Pakistan and India, safeguarding fundamental rights and strengthening humanitarian cooperation to achieve a political settlement.
Historian and author Sinan İlhan examined Kashmir's historical and cultural heritage, particularly its connections with Central Asia and the Turkic world.
He highlighted how centuries of cultural, religious and commercial exchanges helped shape the region's identity.
Journalist and researcher Mehmet Öztürk, who moderated the discussion, focused on the strategic importance of the Indus Waters Treaty and its relationship to the Kashmir dispute.
Öztürk urged both sides to address water-sharing disagreements through diplomacy and international law rather than using shared water resources as political leverage.
Participants concluded by emphasizing sustained diplomatic engagement and a lasting political settlement that respects the rights and aspirations of the Kashmiri people.

articles.title: EU proposes expanded Frontex powers beyond bloc's borders
articles.summary: The European Commission on Tuesday unveiled plans to significantly broaden the authority of EU border agency Frontex, including allowing operations outside the bloc, following a su...
articles.full_text:
The European Commission on Tuesday unveiled plans to significantly broaden the authority of EU border agency Frontex, including allowing operations outside the bloc, following a surge in migrant arrivals at Spain's Ceuta enclave last summer.
The proposal would significantly broaden Frontex's mandate, allowing it to carry out deportations between non-EU countries, operate outside the bloc and deploy rapid-reaction teams in emergencies.
The proposed legislation is an attempt to make Frontex more reactive to large-scale arrivals at the EU's borders, such as in Ceuta on the North African coast, as European governments push for tougher migration policies despite concerns from rights advocates over accountability.
"Today we propose that Frontex becomes the central EU actor on returns," Magnus Brunner, commissioner for internal affairs and migration, told reporters.
"It will be able to act faster, with a quick reaction force that can deploy within 24 hours and spot risks early, before an event becomes a crisis," Brunner added.
But while the proposal would significantly broaden Frontex's role, it would also narrow the scope of its internal rights watchdog, with complaints referred to national authorities to handle.
The proposal comes as member states increasingly focus on returns, arguing that too many migrants ordered to leave the bloc ultimately remain.
Although irregular arrivals have decreased, the arrival of more than 72,000 people in Ceuta from Morocco in late July, most of whom later left, reignited debate over the EU's migration rules and was cited by several member states as evidence for stronger tools.
The plan envisages gradually expanding Frontex's standing corps to 30,000 officers by creating a new "European border and return reserve" of 17,000 officers by 2041, who would remain at the disposal of member states and could be deployed when needed, the commission said in a statement.
The proposal would create a new EU Return Coordination Centre within Frontex and expand the agency's role across the entire deportation process, from voluntary return counselling to organising returns and reintegration support, the statement said.
The agency would also be empowered to help organise and carry out deportations from one non-EU country to another, subject to agreements with the countries involved and international legal standards, according to the statement.
That would mean Frontex could, for example, deport a Bangladeshi national from Libya - one of the main launching points for migrant boats crossing to Europe - back to Bangladesh.
The proposal would also create a new online monitoring centre to track border-related developments on social media and support action against content linked to border security risks.
The Commission proposed allocating €11.8 billion to Frontex for the EU's 2028-2034 budget cycle, nearly double the almost €6 billion earmarked for the agency under the current 2021-2027 framework, as part of a planned expansion of its mandate.
The push comes just a few months after EU lawmakers approved new rules aimed at speeding up deportations and allowing member states to establish return hubs outside the bloc.
Tuesday's proposal was met with criticism from rights groups and some lawmakers.
"Working with third countries, without proper oversight or accountability, is a threat to fundamental rights and respect for international law, while leaving Frontex staff in legal limbo outside of European law," said Tineke Strik, a Dutch MEP from the Greens/EFA group.
"The Commission is pandering to populism and the far right on migration," she added.

articles.title: Ukraine's top diplomat calls for renewed push for peace talks
articles.summary: Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha on Tuesday urged fresh efforts to revive peace negotiations aimed at ending the war. "We need ⁠to get new dynamics in our peace efforts, to...
articles.full_text:
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha on Tuesday urged fresh efforts to revive peace negotiations aimed at ending the war.
"We need to get new dynamics in our peace efforts, to speed them up, to find even new momentum, how to get this new energy in our peace efforts," he told reporters.
He said that President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had asked the leaders of Finland and Norway to convey to Russian President Vladimir Putin the necessity of a cease-fire and a Ukraine-Russia summit.
"We welcome such active support for our diplomatic efforts and peace process. This call was coordinated with us, and this is the right approach," Sybiha told reporters.
The leaders of Finland and Norway phoned Putin on Tuesday to urge him to end the war in Ukraine, breaking with a longstanding practice among Western European leaders of shunning direct contact with the Kremlin.
The call by Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Stoere was an attempt to influence the diplomatic process after U.S. President Donald Trump shifted his position in favor of Russia and U.S. ties with Ukraine hit their lowest point in 18 months.
Stoere said he and Stubb had spoken to Putin for about 90 minutes, and then to Ukrainian President Zelenskyy.
In a joint statement, they linked the initiative to planned peace discussions between Russian, Ukrainian and U.S. officials in Abu Dhabi next month, their first since February.
Moscow and Kyiv remain far apart on how to end the war that began with Russia's invasion in February 2022, and long-range airstrikes by both sides have increased this year while battle lines have remained largely static.
"The discussion (with Putin) was frank and substantive. We are neighbouring countries to Russia. The outcome of this war will have a direct impact on our and the broader European security. Ending the war requires direct discussions," Stubb said.
Stoere said he and Stubb had "stressed the importance of de-escalation." Both voiced strong support for Ukraine.
Meanwhile, Sybiha also said that the U.S.-mediated cease-fire in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian town of Oleshky, where residents reported a food crisis, could be a confidence-building measure in a wider peace process.
"If we see results in Oleshky, this can pave the way for other steps in the peace process," he told reporters.

articles.title: EU eyes better preparedness for climate risks with new strategy
articles.summary: The European Commission presented on Tuesday a new climate strategy aiming to better identify droughts, floods, wildfires and other effects of climate change and to manage the risk...
articles.full_text:
The European Commission presented on Tuesday a new climate strategy aiming to better identify droughts, floods, wildfires and other effects of climate change and to manage the risks more effectively.
Climate resilience should be taken into account in all major EU policy areas in the future, the commission said.
"Europe is warming at double the global rate. To become truly climate resilient, we need to adjust and learn along the way," Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said.
"Today, we are presenting a European approach to climate risks, to anticipate, to prepare for and to manage. We are ensuring that climate resilience will be included in policies across the continent, supporting investment, innovation and long-term growth," she added.
A new Climate Resilience Act is intended to ensure that EU countries assess their climate risks and plan their preventive measures using the same basic assumptions.
The specific ways in which the member states protect themselves against heat, drought and flooding will largely remain up to the individual countries, depending on their risks and priorities.
A website entitled the European Climate Viewer will show potential hazards for specific locations and periods. For example, users should be able to identify railway routes that may be particularly exposed to high temperatures or heavy rainfall, allowing targeted protective measures to be planned.
Other platforms will help public authorities identify suitable, proven measures for addressing specific climate risks.
The aim of the initiative is to anticipate the effects of climate change and prevent damage through action at EU, national and local levels, the commission said.
According to the commission's estimates, economic losses caused by climate-related damage amounted to around 200 billion euros ($223 billion) between 2022 and 2025, or 50 billion euros per year.
In September, von der Leyen announced that the initiative would pursue a whole-of-society approach, down to the local level.
According to data from the EU Earth observation programme Copernicus, the past summer was the hottest on record for Western Europe.
Up to Sept. 2, the area of land that burned in wildfires in the EU was almost twice as large as the average for 2006 to 2025.
According to estimates by British scientists, heat killed around 50,000 people in European cities over the summer, more than ever before.
In Germany, some 16,000 people died as a result of heat, according to estimates by the Robert Koch Institute (RKI), a government health agency.

articles.title: Top Indian media dispute Modi's new data privacy rules in top court
articles.summary: India's Supreme Court Tuesday ordered the government to respond to a challenge by news publishers who argue that new data privacy rules threaten press freedom. Prime Minister Naren...
articles.full_text:
India's Supreme Court Tuesday ordered the government to respond to a challenge by news publishers who argue that new data privacy rules threaten press freedom.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government introduced rules last year to implement a personal data protection law, but critics say their sweeping scope risks undermining public interest reporting.
The new rules "fail to provide any exemption for journalistic activity" and "threaten the full spectrum of journalistic activity," a petition from the Digital News Publishers Association (DNPA) said. The DNPA represents some of India's biggest news organizations.
Members include Network18, part of the Reliance conglomerate led by billionaire Mukesh Ambani and NDTV, owned by the Adani Group, founded by Gautam Adani. Both tycoons are close to Modi.
"We think it could impact investigative journalism and compromise sources," Sujata Gupta, with the DNPA, said.
Data privacy laws in many parts of the world, including the European Union, include specific exemptions for journalism.
The law's requirement to disclose all personal data processed, without a public interest exemption, would "seriously hinder investigative reporting and could discourage whistleblowers from coming forward," Reporters Without Borders, an international media watchdog, said.
Independent activists and smaller news organizations also challenged provisions removing exemptions for personal information sought under India's Right to Information (RTI) transparency law.
"The removal of the public interest override ... of the RTI Act now allows information offices of the government to withhold information that is deemed 'personal' even if it has significant connection to a public activity or public interest," a legal challenge filed by investigative news website The Reporters' Collective argued.
Critics have long accused Modi's Hindu nationalist government of undermining press freedom, a charge the government denies. The court will hear the matter next on Nov. 17.

articles.title: Tit-for-tat Sudan drone strikes kill 21, cause mass power outages
articles.summary: Retaliatory drone strikes between Sudan's warring factions killed at least 21 people in Darfur and caused widespread power outages in the east, witnesses and medics said Tuesday. A...
articles.full_text:
Retaliatory drone strikes between Sudan's warring factions killed at least 21 people in Darfur and caused widespread power outages in the east, witnesses and medics said Tuesday.
A drone strike on a market in Nyala, the de facto capital of Sudan's paramilitary Rapid Support Forces in Darfur, killed 21 people and wounded at least 40 others, a medical source and witnesses said.
One Nyala resident said a market in the city's north was struck by a drone on Monday around 8:00 p.m. (6 p.m. GMT).
Another said the market was frequented by young men, particularly Rapid Support Forces (RSF) fighters.
"Twenty-one people were killed in last night's bombing, and more than 40 others injured," a medic at Nyala Hospital said, though he was unable to identify how many were RSF fighters.
Sudan's military, at war with the RSF since April 2023, regularly strikes Nyala, where the RSF has declared an administration rivaling the army-backed internationally recognized government in Khartoum.
The RSF has in turn launched repeated strikes targeting Khartoum's airport, as well as dams and power stations across the country's east.
On Tuesday, "RSF militia drones targeted the Al-Markhiyat transformer station, disrupting the power supply across large parts of Khartoum and Al-Jazira states," a source in the national electricity company said on condition of anonymity.
The strike comes a day after a coordinated RSF drone attack on six power stations left millions without power in Al-Jazira, White Nile, Sennar and Gedaref states.
The war is currently being fought primarily via drones, with both sides launching sophisticated attacks from across the country, killing dozens of civilians at a time.
In the first three weeks of October alone, drone strikes killed over 300 people and injured hundreds more, according to a U.N. tally.
Since it began, the war has killed more than 200,000 people, aid workers estimate and has triggered the world's largest humanitarian crises.
The United Nations has repeatedly warned that attacks on power stations threaten health and services for millions of people.
Close to 3 million people have returned to Khartoum state since it was recaptured by the army last year, but many have struggled to rebuild their lives in a scarred city.
Power and water supplies remain unreliable, much of the capital remains unsafe from unexploded bombs and many struggle to put food on the table in a collapsed economy.
On Monday, 30 countries including the United States, France and the United Kingdom warned that urgent action was needed to prevent famine expanding across the country.
Sudan is facing "an alarming deterioration" of food security, they said, citing the war, a currency in freefall, higher fuel prices due to the Middle East war and a drought induced by the El Nino climate phenomenon.
Sudan's Foreign Ministry Monday insisted the country's food security was "reassuring," in an attempt to "refute claims of famine."
It accused "some countries and organizations" of "politically exploiting the humanitarian situation."
The army has for years denied claims of documented famine and has been accused of blocking access to humanitarian aid.

Russia and Ukraine began a regional cease-fire Tuesday to launch a humanitarian mission in occupied Oleshky, though fighting persisted elsewhere, including the capital of Kyiv.
The cease-fire is intended to enable aid deliveries and evacuations from the frontline southern Ukrainian town, which faces acute shortages of food and medicine.
"As head of the Ukrainian negotiating team, I confirm that the Ukrainian side is honoring its commitments," Dmytro Lubinets, the parliamentary commissioner for human rights, said on Facebook, confirming the halt's timing.
On Telegram, Russia's Defense Ministry said it stopped shelling toward the Ukrainian city of Kherson starting at 4 a.m. Moscow time (1 a.m. GMT) to prepare for the Oleshky effort; Oleshky faces Kherson across the Dnipro River.
Lubinets added the deal was reached in coordination with U.S. first lady Melania Trump and Russia's commissioner for human rights, Yana Lantratova.
New strikes Tuesday hit the Southern Bridge and subway infrastructure in Kyiv, forcing traffic suspension, city officials said. A Reuters witness heard explosions.
Oleshky lies on the Dnipro's eastern bank in Ukraine's southern Kherson region, opposite Kherson, held by Ukrainian forces.
Russian troops have controlled the town since seizing it in the early days of their February 2022 invasion.
White House envoys talked with both sides in recent days to find a solution as the U.S. seeks to mediate a peace deal to end the war, Europe's deadliest conflict since World War II.
Friday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said peace negotiators from Ukraine, Russia and the United States agreed to meet at a technical level in early November in Abu Dhabi to continue the talks.
Since Monday evening, a Russian missile attack on Kyiv killed at least one person and injured 15, including students in a dormitory. The attacks also killed and injured people in Kharkiv and Pavlohrad.
On Telegram, the Russian Defense Ministry said it hit transport infrastructure in Kyiv, a logistics hub in Kharkiv region, as well as industrial facilities and cargo vessels elsewhere it said were being put to military use.
A drone attack killed one man and wounded six others in the western Russian city of Bryansk, near the Ukrainian border.
A drone hit a bus, killing another person and injuring 30 in the Russian-controlled part of Ukraine's southeastern Zaporizhzhia region, local officials said.
Reuters could not immediately verify the reports. Russia and Ukraine deny deliberately targeting civilians.

articles.title: Jordan kills 20 Daesh terrorists in strikes condemned by Syria
articles.summary: Jordan said Tuesday its airstrikes in southern Syria killed more than 20 Daesh militants and destroyed a weapons depot, while Damascus condemned the operation as a violation of sov...
articles.full_text:
Jordan said Tuesday its airstrikes in southern Syria killed more than 20 Daesh militants and destroyed a weapons depot, while Damascus condemned the operation as a violation of sovereignty and reported several casualties.
Jordanian government spokesperson Mohammad al-Momani said the strikes were conducted after Amman had "run out of patience" with the movements of terrorist groups and threats to its national security.
"The operation was based on field intelligence aimed at neutralizing confirmed threats and planned terrorist attacks against Jordan," he said.
"Initial results of this operation indicate significant losses among ISIS (Daesh), estimated at more than 20 members, as well as the destruction of a major weapons depot belonging to the group," Momani said.
He expressed regret over civilian casualties, saying Jordan refrained from striking locations where intelligence indicated civilians were present.
"Jordan takes precautions to avoid harming civilians and attaches the same importance to the lives of innocent civilians outside its borders as it does to the lives of Jordanians," he said.
Al-Momani said Jordanian authorities were following up on the matter with their Syrian counterparts.
He said the two countries would establish a joint committee to examine the consequences of the operation and strengthen coordination in combating Daesh while protecting civilians.
The spokesperson stressed that Jordan values its relations with Syria and remains committed to developing cooperation in confronting common challenges.
"Jordan's security and Syria's security are one," he said, adding that combating terrorism remains a shared objective.
Momani also linked the security threats to a recent attack on a church in Jordan's Karak governorate that killed nine people.
He reiterated Jordan's support for Syria's security, unity and stability, particularly in the country's south.
Syria's Foreign Ministry, meanwhile, strongly condemned Jordanian airstrikes targeting several locations in the southern Daraa province a day earlier, saying they were carried out without prior coordination with Damascus.
In a Tuesday statement, the ministry said the attacks killed and injured several people, describing the operation as an "unacceptable violation" of Syrian airspace and national sovereignty.
Syrian authorities had earlier reported that seven people were killed in the strikes.
Damascus also condemned Friday's attack targeting St. George Greek Orthodox Church in Jordan, offering condolences to the victims' families and wishing the injured a speedy recovery.
However, the ministry stressed that the Jordanian military operation inside Syrian territory was unacceptable and violated the principles of good neighborliness and bilateral coordination.
It warned that certain parties were seeking to undermine relations between the two countries and fuel tensions, without elaborating.
The ministry said coordination was underway with Jordan to establish an urgent joint civilian and security committee to investigate the incidents, prevent their recurrence and strengthen security cooperation along their shared border.
